memberwhen it runswhat it gets name—a unique string; the stage registers worlds by name paramsread once, when the world is registeredan array of param declarations (below) init(ctx)when the world becomes active{ container, signals, params }. May be async; createShow() waits for it before the loop starts update(dt, state, io)every framedt in seconds (≤ 0.1), state = { key: value } for every param, io = { signals, … } render()every frame, right after updatenothing; draw from what update stored dispose()when another world is activatedrelease GPU objects, DOM, subscriptions surfaceoptionala phone control-surface layout; modules.remote uses it instead of generating one (Phones) container is an absolutely positioned layer that fills the stage. The stage empties it before every init, so you never clean up DOM someone else left. An exception thrown in update or render is caught and logged ([stage] update: / [stage] render:); the show keeps running.

fieldmeaning keythe name routes, automation and the console use. Required. labelwhat the console shows. Defaults to key. min, maxthe range. Overrides are clamped into it; routes scale into it. defthe value when there is no automation and no override. The core reads only def; autoSurface() alone also understands default. stepsnap overrides to multiples of step; on the timeline a stepped param holds each keyframe instead of interpolating. pulsetrue makes it a trigger instead of a level: the console shows a fire button, a mapped pulse signal (or a continuous signal crossing 0.5 upward) fires it, and the world listens with params.onPulse(key, cb). A pulse param has no value in state. groupa label for grouping. Engine params use 'sound'; autoSurface() makes one phone page per group. optionsnames for the values of a stepped param (['Circle', 'Petal', 'Star']); the phone surface shows them as a radio. surfacea hint for the phone surface: { type, color, label }. If two registered worlds declare the same key, they share one param (the first declaration wins).

Continuous control goes through params. Events may use signals. If your world reads signals.get('midi/cc/74') directly in update(), it still works — today, with your controller. But it can no longer be driven by the timeline, by a dancer, or by someone else's controller profile. You've welded the performance to one input. Route it: declare a param, let the mapper connect midi/cc/74 → yourParam, and the same world works for everyone. Events are different: "a note was struck", "a chord resolved", "an onset hit" are moments, not levels. Subscribing to those in init() is correct and encouraged — that's what makes worlds reactive rather than just modulated. Useful event signals: midi/note/on and midi/note/off (any keyboard, the on-screen piano, the simulated performer, a phone), chord/event (one analysis per played gesture), audio/onset, audio/kick, drum/kick. The full list is in the Signals reference.

The timeline is configured next to the world, in the createShow() call: jsCopy Keyframes are [seconds, value], sorted by time. Before the first keyframe the value is the first value; after the last, the last value. Scenes are sorted by t. title and note are what the performer reads in performance mode (T); the next scene and a countdown show under them. A scene with a negative t is a pre-show standby: with t: -30 the clock starts at -0:30. Try performing your world with only the timeline. If it is boring, a param is missing. More in Show control.
The stage does not own a renderer. Build one in init, destroy it in dispose.

createCanvas(container, { alpha = false }) from @openav/stage returns { canvas, ctx, fit, dispose }. fit() keeps the canvas the size of its container (device pixel ratio capped at 2) and returns { w, h } in CSS pixels; call it at the top of render(). Examples 01, 02, 03, 07, 08 and 09 use it.

Load p5 with a script tag in the example's index.html, then run it in instance mode inside the container. p5 draws on its own loop, so update only stores the state and render stays empty (examples 05 and 06): htmlCopy jsCopy

No bundled example uses three.js yet; this is the pattern. Add three to the example's import map ("three": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.160.0/build/three.module.js"), keep the renderer on this, and dispose everything: jsCopy

webtoeWorld() from @openav/world-webtoe turns a WebToe node patch into a world. The patch runs in an iframe; every frame in which a param changed, the resolved params are posted into it, and any patch parameter written as ext('name', fallback) listens (example 04): jsCopy Options: name (default 'webtoe'), app (default https://webtoe.openaudiovisual.com/), project, params, extra.
Anything you append to container is fine. The stage only calls your functions.
jsCopy All worlds' params are registered up front, so the console and the timeline can address any of them. stage.activate(name) does nothing if that world is already active.

update(dt, state, io) receives io. With createShow(), io holds only signals; add output handles once the show exists, and every world sees them: jsCopy Then, inside the world: jsCopy Often it is simpler to do it at the assembly level instead, as example 05 does: show.signals.on('midi/note/on', ({ note, vel }) => show.midi?.noteOn(note, Math.round(vel * 127), 1)). For instruments inside the page (a grand piano, mallets, strings, organ, synth presets), use modules.sound (Show control).

every continuous control is a param (try performing your world with ONLY the timeline) dispose() releases GPU objects and event subscriptions (worlds get switched live) world survives dt spikes (the Loop clamps to 100ms, but don't assume 16ms) nothing in the world reads the clock directly — the timeline owns time the page loads with zero console errors, and works with only the on-screen piano

Every input does one thing: publish signals. With createShow() you switch inputs on in modules; each one is also a plain class you can use on its own. The exact names and ranges are in the Signals reference. inputpackagemodules keydefaultpublishes MIDI hardware@openav/midimidion (false turns it off)midi/… on-screen MIDI controllers@openav/midimidi: { controllers }offmidi/<device>/<control> on-screen piano, QWERTY, simulated performer@openav/keyskeyson (false removes it)midi/note/on, midi/note/off drum machine@openav/drumsdrumsoffdrum/…, midi/note/on on channel 10 microphone@openav/audioaudiooffaudio/… chord analysis@openav/chordchordoffchord/… body (camera)@openav/poseposeoffpose/… hands (camera)@openav/posehandsoffhand/… hands (Leap Motion)@openav/leapleapoffleap/… phones and iPads@openav/remoteremoteoffphone/…, surface/…, midi/note/… Sources that need permission or a user gesture (microphone, camera) are created by createShow() but only start when you click their button in the console's L1 · Input panel: 🎤 mic, 🖐 hands, 🕺 body.

createShow() creates a Midi engine and calls enable() on startup, so the browser may ask for MIDI permission when the page opens. Devices can be plugged in and out during the show; the L1 · Input panel lists them, and unticking one mutes it without unplugging it. Every incoming message publishes two families of names: legacy (what most worlds use, any channel): midi/note/on and midi/note/off pulses, midi/cc/<n> (0..1), midi/bend (−1..1); per channel: midi/ch/<ch>/cc/<n>, midi/ch/<ch>/note/<n> (velocity 0..1 while held, 0 on release), midi/ch/<ch>/bend, midi/ch/<ch>/pressure, midi/ch/<ch>/poly/<n>. A note-on payload is { note, vel, velocity, ch, device }: vel is 0..1, velocity is the raw 1..127, ch is 1..16, device is the port's slug. With two or more devices connected, each also publishes under its own slug so their controls do not collide: midi/<slug>/cc/<n>, midi/<slug>/note/on, midi/<slug>/note/off, midi/<slug>/bend. The slug comes from the port name (Arturia MiniLab 3 → arturia-minilab-3; a second identical unit gets -2), so a device that drops out and comes back keeps its routes. The legacy names keep publishing too, so a route on midi/cc/74 hears every device. Clock messages are ignored. Program change, transport and SysEx are not published (SysEx access is never requested). Using it without createShow(): jsCopy filterOut is a case-insensitive regular expression on input port names that are ignored. The default, 'IAC', keeps the macOS IAC bus out, because a show that sends MIDI out through IAC would otherwise hear itself. See Troubleshooting if you want to receive from IAC. MIDI output is described in Show control.

modules: { midi: { controllers: { profile: '<profile id>' } } } adds an on-screen picture of a known controller. Plug that controller in and the picture switches to it and moves with your hands; without one, play the picture with a mouse or a finger. Its controls publish midi/<device>/<control> names, and controllerRoutes() writes the routes that connect them to params. The MIDI controllers & embedding chapter covers profiles, learning unknown devices, LED feedback and embedding; the supported devices are on the controllers page.

@openav/keys is on by default. It mounts a piano above the console with two checkboxes, keyboard (QWERTY capture) and simulate performance. Options (modules.keys): base (lowest note, default 48), octaves (default 2), sim (show the simulate checkbox, default true), capture (show the keyboard checkbox, default true). It publishes midi/note/on { note, vel, ch: 0 } and midi/note/off { note, ch: 0 }. Note the differences from hardware: ch is 0 and there is no velocity or device field. A world that only reads note and vel works with both. QWERTY (after ticking keyboard): A W S E D F T G Y H U J K O L P ; play 17 notes a semitone apart, starting at base; Z/X move an octave (base stays between 24 and 84); Shift adds 20 to the velocity. While capture is on, the piano claims every letter key (preventDefault); Space, arrows and digits pass through to the console. The simulated performer (SimPlayer) plays a pentatonic scale an octave above base: mostly steps, sometimes leaps and triads, real rests. From code: show.keys.sim.toggle(true). jsCopy

modules: { drums: true } adds a 16-step, four-lane sequencer (kick, snare, hat, clap) with patterns (four on floor, breakbeat, half time, latin, sparse), a tempo slider (60–180 BPM, default 112), swing and humanized timing. Tick drum machine to start it. It plays its own synthesized kit (no samples) and publishes: drum/kick, drum/snare, drum/hat, drum/clap: pulses { level }; drum/<lane>/env: a 0..1 envelope per lane that decays in about 0.12 s, ready to map straight onto a param; midi/note/on { note, vel, ch: 10 } with General MIDI notes (kick 36, snare 38, clap 39, closed hat 42). The shapes match what the microphone's drum detection publishes (audio/kick, audio/kick/env…), so a world mapped to a kick cannot tell a real bass drum from the machine. Example 06 routes both to the same params. Options (modules.drums): engine (another sound engine), autoEnableEngine (default true: the kit's audio engine is switched on by the first hit, no extra click).

modules: { audio: true } creates an AudioAnalyzer; the microphone starts when you click 🎤 mic. (Example 06 writes audio: 'mic'; any truthy value works.) Echo cancellation, noise suppression and auto gain are turned off so the analysis hears the room as it is. Published every frame: audio/rms (smoothed loudness), audio/peak, audio/band/low (20–250 Hz), audio/band/mid (250 Hz–2 kHz), audio/band/high (2–8 kHz), audio/centroid (brightness), and the pulse audio/onset { rms } with a 100 ms refractory time. Drum detection splits transients by band: audio/kick (20–120 Hz), audio/snare (150–800 Hz), audio/hat (6–14 kHz), each a pulse { level } with a matching …/env envelope. Tip Real-world levels rarely reach 1. Speech often sits around 0.05–0.2 RMS and band energies are averages across many FFT bins. Narrow the route's window, for example { source: 'audio/rms', target: 'energy', inMax: 0.3 }. jsCopy

modules: { chord: true } (or { chord: { window: 80 } }) adds a ChordDetector and feeds it every midi/note/on and midi/note/off. It groups notes struck within window milliseconds (default 80) into one gesture and publishes, per gesture: chord/consonance (−1..1), chord/count (number of notes), chord/root (lowest MIDI note); chord/event, a pulse carrying the whole analysis: fieldmeaning notes, count, root, vel, pcssorted notes, how many, the lowest, mean velocity (0..1), pitch classes consonancemean of pairwise interval weights, −1..1 (a single note is 1) isConsonant, isDissonanttwo or more notes and consonance > 0.25 / < −0.15 isTriadthe chord type is major, minor, sus2, sus4, dim or aug thirdsFractionshare of adjacent gaps that are 3 or 4 semitones ("genuinely stacked thirds") dissonanceLevel0 none · 1 mild (a storm warning) · 2 severe (a true cluster) chordTypesingle, major, minor, sus2, sus4, dim, aug, maj7, min7, dom7, halfdim7, maj9, min9, dom9, six, min6, cluster, or chord This is not a music-theory library; it is a performance-semantics layer built for a piece where consonance makes a garden flourish and clusters make it decay (example 02). detector.analyze(notes, vels) is a pure function you can call yourself.

modules: { pose: true } adds a PoseTracker (one body), modules: { hands: true } a HandTracker (two hands, 21 points each, and a gesture for each). The camera starts when you click 🕺 body or 🖐 hands. Both use MediaPipe Tasks Vision (1.2.3), loaded from jsDelivr with its model from Google's storage the first time you enable it; the inference runs on your machine and no video leaves it. The view is mirrored by default (mirror: true), like a mirror on stage, and y is flipped so 1 means raised. Body: pose/present, pose/hand/left/x|y, pose/hand/right/x|y (wrists), pose/hand/left/v, pose/hand/right/v (wrist speed), pose/hands/spread, pose/height (nose height: crouch ↔ stand), pose/lean (−1..1). Hands, per side: hand/<side>/present, hand/<side>/x|y (palm), hand/<side>/tip/x|y (index fingertip), hand/<side>/thumb/index|middle|ring|pinky (thumb tip to each fingertip, 0 = touching, 1 = wide open), hand/<side>/openness (0 = fist, 1 = all fingers out), hand/<side>/angle (0.5 = fingers up, 0.75 = pointing right), hand/<side>/speed. The first measures, hand/<side>/pinch/index|middle and hand/<side>/spread, stay as they were (an open hand reads about 0.5 on them; example 03 plays them). A pinch, as an event: hand/<side>/pinch-start and pinch-end (pulses, with the fingertip's x and y), and hand/<side>/pinched (0/1). Thumb and index must come closer than 0.35 hand sizes with the other three fingers out, so a fist is not a pinch; it ends above 0.56. Gestures: MediaPipe's seven, hand/<side>/gesture/fist|open|point|thumb-up|thumb-down|victory|iloveyou (0/1, and a …-start pulse each), and hand/<side>/gesture (0 none, 1–7 in that order). A gesture starts when its score goes above 0.5 and ends below 0.35. Both hands: hand/both/present, hand/both/distance (palm to palm), hand/both/x|y (the midpoint), hand/both/angle (0.5 = level). Every distance is divided by the size of the hand and measured with x × the frame's aspect ratio, so moving toward the camera or turning the hand sideways does not change a pinch. A closed pinch reads near 0: use invert: true on the route when closing should raise the value (example 03). A pulse plays a pulse param through a route, { source: 'hand/right/gesture/victory-start', target: 'turn' }, so a gesture can cue a scene the way a pad does (example 27). The thresholds were tuned on one performer's hands at a desk, with a TouchDesigner module that uses the same maths. MediaPipe's gesture scores reached only 0.5–0.82 there, which is why a gesture starts at 0.5 and not at the 0.7–0.8 many demos use. Another camera, another distance, another room:…

modules: { leap: true } adds a LeapInput. Browsers cannot read the sensor, so one small bridge per machine does: node packages/leap/bridge/leap-bridge.mjs (needs Ultraleap Hand Tracking installed; --mock gives two animated hands without a sensor; bash packages/leap/bridge/install.sh keeps it running at login on macOS). It serves ws://127.0.0.1:6437 on loopback only. The console's L1 · Input panel shows which link is missing (bridge, tracking service, device) and draws the hands; its simulate button turns the mouse into hands. Signals: per side, leap/hand/<side>/present, x|y|z (palm in the interaction box, 0..1, y up, z toward you), pinch, grab, roll|pitch|yaw (radians), speed, fingertips leap/hand/<side>/<finger>/x|y|z; leap/hands, leap/both/distance, leap/status; pulses pinch-start|pinch-end, grab-start|grab-end per side and leap/both/pinch-start|pinch-end, with hysteresis (a pinch starts above 0.86 and ends below 0.5). Joints for drawing the hand are on leap.hands. The same bridge answers old leap.js sketches on /v6.json, and serves raw hand lines on /raw (example 12, package README).

modules: { remote: true } lets phones join the show over the relay that serve.js hosts. Their sensors publish phone/<id>/… (tilt, acceleration, rotation, knocks, touch, light), mirrored to phone/any/…; the control surface publishes surface/<page>/<widget>; the phone's piano publishes midi/note/on|off like a keyboard. The show page itself can read its own motion sensors on a phone with localSensors(). Everything is in Phones, relay & surfaces.

An input is anything that calls signals.set() or signals.pulse(). Here is the pointer as an instrument: jsCopy Name it source first (breath/pressure, weather/wind), declare its range, and everything downstream (meters, learn, routes, the phone surface) works without changes.
The mapping layer is where "what happened" becomes "what it means". The Mapper (@openav/mapping) is the only component that connects signals to params, and everything it knows is a list of routes.

A route is a plain object. Only source and target are required; addRoute() fills in the rest: fielddefaultmeaning source—signal name, e.g. midi/cc/74, hand/right/pinch/index, phone/any/tilt/x target—param key, e.g. bloom, sound/cutoff inMin, inMax0, 1the window of the signal that is used; values outside it are clamped outMin, outMaxthe param's min, maxthe range written into the param curve'linear'linear, exp, log or smooth invertfalseflip the normalized value (1 − x) before the curve smooth0glide time in seconds (0 = instant) mode(absent = 'override')'override' replaces the timeline's value, 'trim' adds to it, 'pickup' takes over only once the knob has met the value: Trim, pickup and release release(absent = never)seconds the signal must stand still before the route lets go and the timeline plays again enabled(absent = on)false mutes the route idassigneda number, used to remove the route jsCopy In createShow(), the same objects go in routes: [...].

When a signal arrives, every enabled route whose source matches runs these steps, in order: Window: x = (value − inMin) / (inMax − inMin), clamped to 0..1. Invert: if invert, x = 1 − x. Curve: x = curve(x). Scale: out = outMin + (outMax − outMin) · x. Write: with smooth: 0, the param is overridden with out (and clamped and snapped to its step). With smooth > 0, out becomes a target that mapper.update(dt) glides toward every frame. A trim route writes the timeline's value plus out; a pickup route writes nothing until the knob has met the param.

curveformulafeel linearxas the hand moves expx²slow start, fast end: fine control near the bottom log√xfast start, slow end: fine control near the top smoothx²(3 − 2x)gentle at both ends (smoothstep) An unknown curve name falls back to linear.

inMin/inMax say which part of the signal matters; outMin/outMax say where it lands. Typical uses: a bipolar signal: { source: 'midi/bend', inMin: -1, inMax: 1 }, or a phone tilt { source: 'phone/any/tilt/x', inMin: -1, inMax: 1 }; a quiet signal: { source: 'audio/rms', inMax: 0.3 } uses the whole param range for the levels a voice actually reaches; a knob that only sweeps part of a param: { source: 'midi/cc/1', target: 'hue', outMin: 180, outMax: 270 }; an inverted relation without invert: outMin: 1, outMax: 0. Warning outMin/outMax default to the target param's range at the moment the route is added. If the param does not exist yet, they default to 0..1. In createShow(), routes are added before the sound engine registers its sound/* params, so a declared route to sound/cutoff needs explicit outMin: 100, outMax: 8000.

smooth is a time constant in seconds: after smooth seconds the param has covered about 63% of the distance to the new value (a one-pole filter, k = 1 − e^(−dt/smooth) per frame). 0.05–0.15 hides the steps of a MIDI knob or a 30 Hz phone stream; 0.2–0.5 makes a hand feel heavy. The glide starts from the param's current value (a value set by hand, else what the timeline says right now, see base), so the first movement never jumps, and it stops writing once it has arrived.

When the target is a pulse param, the route fires it instead of writing a value: a pulse source (midi/note/on, audio/kick, drum/kick, phone/any/knock…) fires it on every event; a continuous source fires it when the normalized value crosses 0.5 upward (a phone-surface button going from 0 to 1, a fader pushed past the middle). curve, invert, smooth and the output range do not apply to pulse targets.

One signal may drive many params (add several routes with the same source), and one param may listen to many signals. When two routes write the same param, the last one to write wins. Learn adds a route; it never replaces one. The patch bay design plans per-route combine (last, max, add, avg) and label fields; they are not implemented yet.

A route writes its param as an override, and overrides are sticky: as soon as a mapped signal moves, the timeline stops driving that param. Clearing the override (✕ next to the param, or show.params.clearOverride(key)) hands it back to the timeline until the signal moves again. A smoothed route writes only while it is gliding. Once it has arrived it stops, so ✕ (or a slider you drag) takes the param back and it stays back until the knob moves again; ✕ in the middle of a glide stops the glide. The mapper notices when something else has written the param since its own last write, the same number included, and stands down. "Moves again" means a change: a source that sends the same reading again (the relay does, once a second, for every phone control) does not take the param back. The rule behind this is Who holds a value. Muting a route stops it writing; the param keeps the value it had (a muted trim gives its offset back). A replacing route throws the timeline's curve away for as long as it holds the param. For a knob that should nudge the timeline, or hand it back when you let go, read on.

Three route fields change who wins when a knob meets a timeline. All three are off unless you write them: a route without mode and release is the replacing route described above. fieldwhat the knob does mode: 'override'the default: the knob's value replaces the timeline's, until ✕ mode: 'trim'the knob's value is an offset added to the timeline's value, which keeps moving underneath mode: 'pickup'like override, but the knob only takes over once it has met the param's current value release: 4with any mode: when the knob has stood still for 4 seconds, let go and let the timeline play mode and release do not apply to pulse targets.

trim, pickup and the start of a smooth glide all need the timeline's value for the param right now. The mapper takes it from base, a function that answers { key: value }: jsCopy timeline.state() is the value before overrides, with a score's segment modules already applied, which is what the param would be if nobody touched it. Without base the mapper uses the param's def: right for a param nothing automates, wrong for one the timeline draws. A base that throws or answers something else is treated as absent; it never stops the show. Keep it cheap: it is asked every frame while a trim holds a param, and at each reading of a trim or pickup knob.

For a work whose timeline already draws the whole show, turning a knob to 0.9 should not throw the curve away. A trim route's outMin/outMax are an offset range, and the param is timeline value + offset, clamped to the param's range. Without them the knob spans half the param's range each way (knob in the middle = no change): jsCopy The offset rides on the timeline: when the curve moves, the param moves with it, every frame. smooth smooths the offset (it starts from 0, never from a jump). Two trim routes on one param add up, so a coarse and a fine knob work together. A trim on a param that also has a replacing route sits on top of the replacing route's value. While a trim holds a param, the param is overridden: the console shows it with a ✕, and a timeline.record source that reads the override gets the sum, what the audience saw. ✕ clears the offset; the knob's next move brings it back. Removing or muting the route gives the param back at once.

A knob and a parameter rarely start in the same place. With mode: 'pickup' the route writes nothing until the knob's value has met the param's current value: within 2% of the route's output range, or crossed over it between two readings. From then on it behaves like a replacing route, gliding from where the param was (no jump). The comparison uses the value the param has right now, so it works while the timeline moves. A release or ✕ puts the route back to "not met yet".

release: 4 means: when the signal has not moved for 4 seconds, the route lets go. Movement is a change of more than 0.1% of the input window, measured from where it last counted as moved, so a slow drift counts and a source that keeps sending the same value does not. Then: with smooth: 0 the param goes back to the timeline at once; with smooth > 0 it fades into the timeline over about three times smooth seconds, then the override is cleared (a trim fades its offset to zero); the route waits until the source moves again before it takes anything: a source that keeps repeating the same value does not take the param back; it only clears what it wrote itself. If a slider took the param over in the meantime, that stays. jsCopy

One param can have several writers: the timeline, a few routes, the console's slider, the work's own code. An engine value has one more, the per-frame push of the sound/* params into the sound engine. Since 0.11.0 one rule decides between them, and every writer in the framework follows it: The last deliberate change wins, and a repetition is not a change. A value set by hand holds until it is released, or until a source really moves. createShow({ writes: 'legacy' }) brings back exactly how 0.10.0 wrote: every sound/* value into the engine every frame, a route that takes its param back on any reading after ✕ or a slider, a glide that only notices a hand writing a different number. new Mapper({ …, writes: 'legacy' }) and new Sound({ …, writes: 'legacy' }) do the same for a mapper or a sound shell built by hand. It prints one deprecation warning and will go in a later version; what changed, and how to tell whether a work leaned on it, is in the changelog.

Click learn next to a param in L3 · Params (or call mapper.learn('bloom')), then move something. The mapper binds the first signal that: moves by at least 5% of its declared range from where it was when learn started (a knob, a fader, a hand, a phone tilt), or fires, if it is a pulse (a key, a pad, a knock). The new route has the defaults: linear, no smoothing, the param's full range. Edit it afterwards if it needs a curve. Clicking learn again cancels. Learn adds: a param that already has a route keeps it and gets a second one. To bind a whole list, the L2 · Mapping panel has 🎛 map knobs in order: it arms learn for the first param, you turn one knob, it is bound and the next param is armed. skip, back, stop (or Esc) steer it. In code it is LearnWizard (details). Caution Any pulse binds immediately. Untick simulate performance and stop the drum machine before you learn, or the next note they play becomes the route. When one MIDI message publishes several names (midi/cc/74, midi/ch/1/cc/74, and with two devices midi/<slug>/cc/74), learn binds the first one, midi/cc/74, which hears every device. Change the source to the per-device name if you need one device only.
The L2 · Mapping panel lists every route as source → target with a checkbox (mute) and ✕ (remove). In code: jsCopy

The mapper saves its routes to localStorage under openav.map.<profile>. createShow() uses the world's name as the profile (or the profile option) and: loads the saved routes if there are any, otherwise adds the declared routes; when a saved profile exists, still adds every declared route whose source → target pair is missing, so new routes in code arrive; saves every 3 seconds. So learned routes and edits survive a reload. The flip side: if you change the curve or smoothing of a declared route in code, the saved copy of that source → target pair wins. To start clean, pass profile: false (routes come from code on every load, as in example 09) or remove the saved profile: jsCopy To carry a wiring to another machine or another world, use a map file (next section).

The L2 · Mapping panel has three buttons under map knobs in order: ⬇ export downloads the routes as oav-map-<world>.json. ⬆ import picks a map file. You can also drop a .json anywhere on the page. Import replaces the routes; the new set is remembered at once. clear removes every route (click twice). On the next load the world's declared routes come back, as on a first visit. Below the buttons the panel says what the last import did: how many routes came in, and every route it skipped and why. A file that cannot be read says so and changes nothing.

jsonCopy Routes are named by signal and param, never by id, so a file travels between worlds: a route whose param this world does not have is skipped and listed; a route whose signal nothing in this show can produce (say leap/palm/x without a Leap Motion module) is skipped and listed. Signals that only appear when the first message arrives (midi/…, surface/…, phone/…, osc/…, key…, take/…) are kept and counted as waiting; when the file's world is a different one, the range.out is dropped so each param keeps its own range (the in window, curve, smoothing and invert come along); version newer than this build reads is refused with a message. A bare array from mapper.toJSON() (the old way) still imports, as version 0. mode ("trim" or "pickup") and release (seconds) are optional route keys in version 1, written only when a route uses them. A build from before they existed ignores them and reads the route as a replacing route. For a trim route, range.out is the offset range. Files over 256 KB or with over 500 routes are refused.

textCopy ?map=<url> fetches the file when the page opens and loads it like an import. It accepts a same-origin address (relative paths included) or an absolute https one; http: to another host, data:, javascript:, file: and addresses with a login are refused. A cross-site file must be served with CORS (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *; raw GitHub and gists do this). The show starts regardless: if the address is refused, the fetch fails or the file is bad, the panel shows the reason and the routes stay as they were. An explicit ?map= beats the remembered wiring, and what it loads is remembered like any import. In code, createShow({ map: 'maps/a.json' }) does the same and map: false ignores ?map=.

The mapper saves its routes to localStorage (openav.map.<world>) every 3 seconds and right after an import or clear, one slot per world name, so the next visit starts where you stopped. Every read and write is wrapped: in a private window or with storage blocked nothing breaks, the wiring just is not remembered. In code: jsCopy

Several packages generate routes in this same shape: autoSurface(world.params) (@openav/surface) builds a phone control panel and the surface/<page>/<widget> → param routes for it, with smooth: 0.04; routesFromLayout(layout, params) does the same for a hand-written layout (Phones, relay & surfaces). controllerRoutes(profile, { knob1: 'hue', pad1: 'burst' }) (@openav/midi) writes routes from an on-screen controller's controls (MIDI controllers & embedding).
jsCopy onChange() runs when routes change (for UIs); onLearn(route, signalName) runs when learn binds.
The parts that turn a sketch into a performance: the one-call assembly, the timeline, the console, performance mode, the backstage monitor, and the ways sound and data leave the browser.

createShow() (@openav/show) builds a whole show around a world and returns every part. By default a show runs on the page's requestAnimationFrame (with a Web Worker heartbeat for a hidden tab). loop changes who supplies the frames, so a show can be recorded one exact frame at a time, tested as a whole, or run for a night with no window in front of it, without replacing the page's global requestAnimationFrame or performance.now. jsCopy 'auto' (or leave loop out) is the behaviour a show always had. 'manual' schedules nothing. show.loop.step(dt) runs one whole frame (the frame order) of dt seconds. dt is not clamped to 0.1 s (you chose it), 0 redraws in place, and a negative or non-number dt runs nothing and returns false. The time onFrame and show.loop.fps see is virtual, the sum of the dt stepped, so two runs with the same steps are the same run. Nothing is drawn until the first step, and the timeline moves only while it is playing (show.timeline.play()). { clock, raf } keep the loop automatic but take its time from you. clock() returns milliseconds; raf(cb) asks for one callback on the next frame, and cb(now) may be handed the timestamp (without one, clock() is read). The Worker heartbeat is off, because a real timer must not step a fake clock; heartbeat: true turns it back on. maxDt still clamps these frames. Only the frame loop is yours. Date.now, setTimeout, the mapper's auto-save, Web MIDI and the audio engine keep real time, and the backstage feed throttles itself by the wall clock, so a recording pairs loop: 'manual' with monitor: false. A show you assemble by hand does the same with new Loop(fn, { manual: true }) (@openav/core).

At a hold, play() and toggle() release it seek(t)jump to t seconds (clamped between the first scene's negative time, or 0, and total) jumpScene(d)go to the start of the scene d steps away next(), prev()→ and ←: next() releases a hold (and plays on), otherwise it is jumpScene(1) release()let a hold go: the next scene starts and playback continues. false when nothing was holding reset()stop, clear a hold and rewind to start (default 0) advance(dt)per frame; moves t by dt × rate while playing state(t), valueAt(key, t)the automation values at a time (no overrides) sceneIndexAt(t), currentScene(t), sceneEnd(i)scene lookup onSceneChange(cb)cb(index, scene, { cause }) whenever playback or a seek lands in a different scene; cause is 'play', 'release', 'seek', 'jump', 'reset' or 'loop' onCue(cb), cues(), fireCue(cue)scene cues fired by playback, the list of them, and the manual trigger loop, onLoop(cb), loopRange(), loopswrap the show, a scene or a range record(key, source), stopRecording(), onRecord(cb), mergeTake(key, take)write a value source into a lane onSeek(cb)cb(t, kind) when the playhead is moved by hand ('seek', 'jump', 'reset'), never while playing lanePos(t), laneTime(id, p), lanePlan(), lanes()automation seconds ↔ (segment id, progress p), the segment table, and the automation written per segment exportAutomation(opts), importAutomation(doc, opts)the automation as plain JSON, in seconds or per segment, and back anchor(epoch, opts), unanchor(), drift(), onDrift(cb)read the wall clock: count how far behind it the show runs, warn, catch up, start on schedule layer(key, value, t) => value: rewrite a param…

Curves. A keyframe is [t, value, curve?]. The third item says how the segment that ends at that keyframe gets there: 'linear' (the default: leave it out and you get what the timeline always did), 'ease' (slow, fast, slow), 'in' (starts slow), 'out' (starts fast), 'step' (hold the old value until the keyframe, then jump), or your own function of 0..1. CURVES is exported. A param with step still holds, whatever the curve says. jsCopy Loop. loop: true wraps at total (back to 0) and keeps playing; 'scene' repeats the scene the playhead is in (next() moves the loop on to the next scene); a scene id loops that scene; { from, to } loops a range in seconds or scene ids. It is a property: timeline.loop = !timeline.loop is the whole L key. onLoop(cb) tells you each lap, and a loop that wraps into another scene is an onSceneChange with cause: 'loop'. A hold inside the range still holds. Cues. scene.cues is [{ name, t }] (the console scrubber already draws them as ticks). onCue((cue, { cause }) => …) fires one when playback passes it, once, and never when you seek, jump, drag the scrubber or reset: a scrub is not a performance. Each lap of a loop fires them again. fireCue(cue) sets one off by hand. With a score the director fires its own cues; use onCue on plain timelines. jsCopy Recording. record(key, source) arms a lane. While the timeline plays, source() is read every frame: a number is written into a take, null means nobody is touching and closes it. jsCopy A take also closes on pause, seek, reset, a hold, the end of the show and the end of each loop lap, while the recorder stays armed until stop() / stopRecording(). The merge rule (mergeTake()): the take is thinned (a point stays when it moved more than 0.6 % of the param's range, or 0.5 s passed), and it replaces the keyframes inside its time span. Keyframes outside stay, so the lane glides from the previous keyframe to the take's first point, and from its last point to the next keyframe. Existing curves outside the take are untouched. With a score the keyframes are written in the base cut's time, like the ones you declared. A cue list is just a scene-change handler: jsCopy

With a score the show is a list of segments whose lengths change, and a curve written in absolute seconds goes stale the moment one of them grows. Write the curve on the segment instead. The automation of a key may be an object: its keys are segment ids, its values are keyframes [p, value, curve?] with p the progress through the segment, 0 to 1. jsCopy A point [p, v, curve] is exactly the keyframe [segment.start + p × segment.dur, v, curve], nothing more: the timeline compiles every lane when it is built, and timeline.automation holds ordinary absolute keyframes, so valueAt, recording, mergeTake and the console behave as before. The desk's Curves panel draws the lanes across the whole show with the segment ids behind them. Any cut. The lane is compiled against the root cut of the score (the cut a derived cut came from). A cut with other lengths reads the same lane with its own lengths, so (dawn, 0.5) is half way through dawn in every cut, and a derived cut (from + scale) is stretched like absolute keyframes. Two cuts that differ in structure, not only in length, can share one lane. Seams. Between the last point of a segment and the first point of the next, the value glides like between any two keyframes (the arriving point's curve applies). For a seamless seam write the same value at p: 1 and at the next segment's p: 0. Two points at the same instant with different values are a jump. Segments a cut lacks. An id that another cut of the score has but this one does not is skipped, so one lane serves a cut with a segment fewer. An id that no cut has (a typo) throws, naming the key and the id; so does a p outside 0…1 or out of order, naming the key, the segment and the point. Without a score the scenes are the segments: a scene lasts until the next one starts.

record() writes a take into timeline.automation, in memory. To keep it, export it as plain JSON and import it later, into this timeline or another: jsCopy jsonCopy exportAutomation({ keys, as, precision }) returns a copy. as: 'seconds' (the default) writes each key as the keyframes in the root cut's seconds; as: 'segments' writes each key as a lane, with p rounded to precision decimals (9; null keeps every digit). The two are inverses: the lanes compile back to the same curve. A keyframe outside the show has no segment, so it can only be exported as seconds, and a curve that is a function cannot be written to JSON at all: both throw, naming the key. cut is the id of the root cut. importAutomation(doc, { keys, replace, ignoreCut }) takes the file, or a bare { key: keyframes | lane } map. It replaces the keys the file has (keys narrows them; replace: true also clears the ones it does not mention). It is all-or-nothing: if one key is bad, nothing changes. Seconds belong to the cut they were written against, so a file whose cut is not this timeline's root cut is refused (ignoreCut: true overrides); lanes are not tied to a cut. The conversion behind it is public. lanePos(t) answers { id, index, p } for a second (null outside the show; a boundary belongs to the segment that starts there), laneTime(id, p) answers the second, lanePlan() is the segment table, and lanes() is the whole automation written per segment. They work in automation seconds, the ones in timeline.automation and in onRecord's from/to. For the playhead's own show seconds use the score: score.locate(T) and score.timeAt(id, p) (Score). The pure functions compileLane, decompileLane, lanePos and laneTime are exported too, for tools that have a segment table [{ id, start, end }] (score.rootSegments) and no timeline.

The frame loop clamps dt to 0.1 s (Architecture). When the page stalls for half a second, the show moves 0.1 s and falls 0.4 s behind the wall clock. On a short show nobody notices; on a night-long installation nobody is there to see how much it has lost. anchor() makes the timeline read the wall clock (Date.now, in milliseconds) on every frame it plays and compare how long the clock ran with how far the show moved. Nothing happens unless you call it: an unanchored timeline never reads a clock. jsCopy anchor(epoch?, opts): epoch is the wall-clock moment of show time 0, as milliseconds, a Date or an ISO string. Leave it out and the first playing frame is time 0: there is nothing to be late for, only the stalls from then on count. optiondefaultmeaning mode'warn''warn' counts and tells, and never moves t. 'catch-up' gives back what was lost, and waits when it runs ahead warnAt1seconds behind at which onDrift hears 'behind' (and console.warn if nobody listens); it hears 'recovered' below half of it tolerance0.05'catch-up': owing less than this is not repaid jump10'catch-up': owing more than this is closed by one seek (no cues fire, the way a seek never fires them), not by racing on waittrue'catch-up': an epoch in the future keeps the show standing still, playing but not moving, until then stall0.02a frame whose wall time exceeds dt by more than this counts as a stall (counting only) nowDate.nowthe clock, in milliseconds; pass the same fake clock you give a test or a manual loop onDriftnonecb({ kind, …drift() }) for 'behind', 'recovered' and 'jump'; timeline.onDrift(cb) adds more What 'catch-up' does: the difference is added to that frame's step, so cues, holds and loops behave as in normal playback (a hold still stops the show). An epoch in the past is a late start: a machine restarted at 20:07 for a show that began at 20:00 lands seven minutes in. A pause, a hold and the end of the show are the show standing still on purpose, so they are not drift: whatever was owed at that moment is forgiven (forgiven) and counting resumes from where the show stands. Running ahead of the wall clock (a negative behind) is only reported in 'warn'; 'catch-up' holds the show back for it (held): it waits for the clock and never runs backwards, which also cancels the extra 0.1 s frame the loop's heartbeat adds right after a stall. reset() starts the counting over; an epoch still in the future survives it. drift() answers null when there is no anchor, otherwise behind (seconds slower than the wall clock; negative = ahead), lost (what the clamp, or any stall, cost), repaid,…

A timeline can chase another timeline's clock instead of walking by itself. That is the timeline's half of several pages performing one show: the leader runs, the followers follow. The source can be anything that answers "where is the leader?": the @openav/sync follower, a recording, a test's fake leader. Nothing happens unless you call follow(): a timeline that never follows runs exactly as it did before. jsCopy follow(source, opts). The source answers with the leader's last frame, { T, playing, holding, rate, at }: T is the leader's time when it sent the frame, at is when the frame arrived here, in milliseconds on the same clock as now (leave it out and the frame counts as arriving this instant). It answers null before it has heard anyone. Every frame the follower works out where the leader is now: T, plus the time since at times rate (nothing is added while the leader is paused or holding), plus latency. optiondefaultmeaning nudge0.05while it catches up, rate is the leader's rate times 1 ± this: a follower 0.3 s behind closes the gap in about six seconds, and nobody sees a jump deadband1/60a difference under one frame is left alone. Past it the nudge starts, and it stops at half of it, so it does not flutter on the edge jump0.5a difference over this many seconds is one seek(T, 'seek'): onSeek hears it and no cue fires lostAfter4seconds without a frame before the leader counts as gone; Infinity waits for ever latency0seconds a frame spends on the way, a number or a function. Set it for pages on different machines (for example half the round trip) nowsource.now, else performance.nowthe clock, in milliseconds; the one the source stamps at with onFollownonecb({ kind, …followStatus() }) for 'found', 'lost' and 'jump'; timeline.onFollow(cb) adds more What the follower copies from the leader: its rate, its pause (the follower stops on the leader's exact T) and its hold. When the leader parks at the end of a hold scene, the follower walks up to the boundary and parks there by itself (its own cues and scene changes fire on the way). It lets go only when the leader's T is past the boundary, so a late frame from just before it cannot release a follower that arrived first. A looping show is followed across the wrap of the loop, by the shorter way round. The leader is the clock: while following, the follower's own play(), pause(), seek() and rate are overruled by the next frame, and anchor() stands aside until unfollow(). When no frame has come for lostAfter seconds the follower runs by itself on the last rate it was given, exactly like a timeline that does not…

mountConsole(el, app, { layers, signals, keys }) (@openav/console) builds the director's desk; createShow() mounts it in the side panel. app is the object createShow() returns as show.app (timeline, params, mapper, signals, stage, midi, sound, audio, hands, pose, …); missing parts simply hide their section. Pass { layers: false } or { signals: false } to leave out those panels. It gives you transport + scrubber with scene blocks, the Layers overview, L1 Input, L2 Mapping, L3 Params (sliders with override and learn chips), L4 sound, live signal meters and a MIDI log. Keyboard: Space play/pause (at a hold: release) · →/← next / previous scene (→ at a hold: release) · R reset · T performance mode · F fullscreen · M the on-screen MIDI controller (midi.controllers) · C the Curves panel · Esc leave keyboard-piano capture or stop the mapping wizard. Keys typed into an input field, held keys and ⌘/Ctrl/Alt combinations are ignored. While the on-screen piano captures the keyboard the letters belong to the piano (T and F are piano keys), so R, T, F and M do nothing until you untick it or press Esc; Space and the arrows always work.

A show that plays the computer keyboard as a piano wants its letters. keys maps each action to a key (or a list of keys), laid over the defaults; false switches one action off, and keys: false switches every shortcut off. jsCopy actiondefaultdoes playSpaceplay / pause (at a hold: release) next, prevArrowRight, ArrowLeftnext / previous scene (next at a hold: release) resetRback to the start; brings back switched-off segment modules perfTperformance mode fullscreenFfullscreen midiMthe on-screen MIDI controller panel cancelEscapestop the mapping wizard, or leave keyboard-piano capture curvesCopen / close the Curves panel (nothing happens while no param is automated) A key is a string. 'r' is the character (either case); 'KeyR' is the physical key whatever the keyboard layout types there (a Zhuyin layout types ㄐ); 'F6', 'Backquote', 'ArrowUp', 'Space' are KeyboardEvent.code or key names, case does not matter. 'Shift+T', 'Ctrl+K', 'Alt+…', 'Meta+…' add modifiers: without Ctrl, Alt or Meta in the spec those must not be held (⌘R and Ctrl+F stay the browser's), and a plain letter ignores Shift. Letters (a–z, ;) stay dead while the piano captures the keyboard, wherever you put them; F6, Backquote and the like work through it. An unknown action name or a malformed key throws before anything is mounted. The hints on the desk (the play button's tooltip, the HOLD banner, the prompter) print the keys you chose; desk.keys (show.console.keys) holds them. With mountConsole by hand, the midi key toggles app.midiPanel when you pass one. With a score the desk also has the Director panel, cue ticks on the scrubber and a prompter with the operator's acts (Score & Director). The L2 Mapping panel has 🎛 map knobs in order, a wizard that arms learn for each param in turn (details). Override semantics: touch a slider (or a mapped control) and that param leaves the timeline's hands until you clear it (✕). Yellow label = overridden. The Curves panel shows the same override on the param's curve and clears it with ↩.

Curves shows what the timeline will do to every param, for the whole show at once. It is a panel on the desk, collapsed at first: its header opens it, and so does C. There is one curve for each param that has automation, time across (the same axis as the scrubber, a standby before 0 included) and the param's range up. Press or drag on a curve or on the ruler to move the playhead, as on the scrubber. A show with nothing automated has no panel. Segments. The ruler names the segments (the score's, or the scenes of a plain timeline) and the curves have their boundaries behind them; a dashed gold line is where a hold waits. A band too narrow for its name keeps it for the hover tip. A derived cut shows the same curves over its own length, and a lane written per segment sits where its segment is. The playhead. A white column, and a ring on the curve where the show is now. The number in the head is the value the show is using this frame. Overrides. A param that a slider, a mapped knob or a phone has taken over is marked amber: a dot where it was taken to, a dashed line across the show, and ↩ in its head, which gives the param back to its curve (the same as ✕ on the Params panel). ↩ all gives back every curve in the view. An override on a param with no curve is not in the view and stays as it is. Recording. The take that timeline.record is writing into a lane is drawn in red while it plays, and the curve is redrawn when the take closes. Cost. Closed, it does nothing: it measures nothing, draws nothing and has not made a canvas. Open, each curve is drawn once, and again only when the automation, the cut or the width changes (an import, a take, an edited keyframe); every frame only the playhead and the overrides are redrawn. Rows scrolled out of the 264 px list are neither drawn nor cleared, so the drawing for fifty automated params is the drawing for about six. It reads the timeline and the params and nothing else, so it works for any show without the work saying anything. jsCopy

T flips to a fullscreen teleprompter: current scene title + note in stage- readable type, what the operator does (the scene's acts), next scene preview, clock + scene countdown, a HOLD banner while the show waits, and a warning when a segment module was switched off. This is for the performer; the audience-facing window is your stage in fullscreen (F). Two windows of the same page = one desk, one stage.

bashCopy Every show page made with createShow() streams snapshots to ws://<the page's host>:7457 about 15 times a second, so run the monitor server on the machine that serves the show. Backstage shows clock, scene, world, FPS, overrides, all signals and params live, and a red "stage feed lost" banner if the stage stops sending for 4 s — which is exactly the moment a stage manager earns their pay. Zero configuration, zero dependencies; both ends reconnect by themselves. GET /health answers { ok, clients }. When no monitor is running, the show page keeps retrying with a growing delay (about 5 s, growing to 30 s); the browser logs each refused connection. That message is expected. A machine that does not need a backstage, or a relay somewhere else, is an option of createShow(): jsCopy monitor: false builds no feed (show.monitor is null) and the page never opens a socket. { url, hz } goes to MonitorFeed: a ws:// or wss:// address (null makes a feed that never connects) and the snapshots per second (default 15). Behind TLS the relay needs a wss:// address, and the relay itself still listens where you started it (node packages/monitor/server.js 7460). For a hand-assembled show: jsCopy

A work can put its own health numbers on the backstage page: the tick its simulation is on, how far it has drifted from the wall clock, how many NaNs it has caught. They travel as snapshot.extra and appear in a Work panel that stays hidden while nothing is sent. A show that sends nothing sends the same snapshot as before. jsCopy A value is a number, a string (80 characters at most), a boolean or null. { v, min, max, warn } draws a meter (with min and max) and turns the row red (warn: true). A name is 48 characters at most and a snapshot carries 64 fields at most. What JSON cannot carry (NaN, a BigInt, a function, a nested object) is dropped or becomes null, so one bad number never costs the frame, and a provider that throws is skipped. monitor() and a function extra are asked every frame, monitor.extra(fn) only when a frame goes out (about 15 a second): keep anything expensive there. On a name two sources share, extra beats the world and a later monitor.extra beats an earlier one.

A wall of three outputs, a stage and a lobby, a rehearsal laptop beside the show laptop: one show, several pages. One page is the leader: it runs the timeline, takes the input, and says every frame where it is. The others are followers: their timelines chase the leader's T (follow), so every page shows the same moment of the same show. Give every page the same code and a different role: jsCopy sync keydefaultmeaning rolerequired'leader' or 'follower' channelrequiredthe name of the BroadcastChannel and of the relay room: 1–32 letters, digits, - or _. Pages on the same channel are one show urlnonenone: a BroadcastChannel (pages of one browser profile and one origin). true: this page's own /relay (node serve.js hosts it). 'ws://host:port/relay': the relay on that machine inputleader true, follower falsewhether this page takes input of its own. Without it the modules that make input are switched off: keys (the keyboard piano), midi, drums, audio, hands, pose, leap, remote. Everything else is yours follow{}follower: the options of timeline.follow() (jump, lostAfter, latency, nudge, onFollow) extra, statenoneleader: data that travels with the clock (below) info, accept, onFrame, onState, onGapnonefollower: hooks and checks (below) hzevery frameleader: at most this many frames a second; a change of state (play, pause, hold, rate, seek) is sent at once aliveEvery, forgetAfter2000, 6000follower: say here every this many ms once it has the state (0 = never). Leader: stop counting a follower that said here and then went quiet this long id, nowrandom, performance.nowthe peer id and the clock Transports. On one machine the pages talk through a BroadcastChannel: no network and nothing to run. The browser connects only pages of the same origin and profile, so open the leader and the followers from the same address. Across machines they join a room on the room relay as role=leader and role=follower; node serve.js on the leader's machine is enough (url: 'ws://<that machine>:8080/relay'). A page served over https needs a wss:// address (the browser blocks ws:// there). The relay has no authentication: use a closed network and a channel name nobody will guess (Security). Both transports carry the same JSON, so a work does not change when the wire does. Messages. The same on both transports; seq counts the leader's frames. textCopy A follower says hello when it comes up, and again every second until it has a state, after a gap in seq, after a silence and whenever its socket reconnects. The leader answers with a state, so a page that joins in the middle, or reloads, is on…

bashCopy The defaults are 7456 127.0.0.1 3456. The browser cannot send UDP, so OscOut posts batches to the bridge over HTTP and the bridge sends them as OSC packets. jsCopy Numbers go out as OSC floats — what Spat, Reaper, and TouchDesigner expect; anything else is sent as a string. Only the latest message per address survives a frame. If the bridge disappears, OscOut reports it through onStatus(ok, info) and stops trying after 30 failed flushes. createShow() does not create an OscOut. Add one yourself (and add "@openav/osc": "../../packages/osc/index.js" to the page's import map): jsCopy

OSC goes to TouchDesigner as above. TouchDesigner can also show an open-audiovisual page as a picture with its Web Render TOP, which draws a web page inside TouchDesigner on the same machine (Web Render TOP). We have not checked whether the Web Render TOP supports Web MIDI or WebGPU. Keep the control on OSC. If the page comes from openaudiovisual.com, Chrome asks before the page may reach the bridge on 127.0.0.1: see Chrome asks about the local network (Chrome blog). Running node serve.js and opening the page from http://localhost:8080 avoids the prompt.

midi.noteOn/noteOff/cc/send go to the selected output port — and midi.panic() sends all-notes-off + all-sound-off + sustain-off + per-note note-offs on all 16 channels, through the same observable throat as everything else. Bind it to a pad you can find in the dark. Every performer eventually needs it; ours is one call. jsCopy The first output port is used until you choose another (enable(preferredOut) matches a name exactly, then as a substring). Everything sent passes through onSend, which feeds the per-channel MIDI OUT meter in the Layers panel. Hot-plug. A cable pulled mid-show must not leave the DAW silent without a word. When the current output is unplugged, Midi moves to the next best live port: the one you chose with selectOutput() or enable(name), then the first match of the prefer list (new Midi({ prefer: ['IAC'] })), then the first port. When the port you chose is plugged in again, the output goes back to it. An unrelated device appearing never steals the output. Every switch prints one line in the MIDI log (the Signals panel, via midi.onMessage) and one in the browser console, flashes in the MIDI controller panel, and updates the MIDI out → row of the L1 Input panel. In code: midi.onOutput(({ text, reason }) => …). Echo. What you send into a virtual bus must not come back as input. Inputs whose name matches filterOut (default IAC, the macOS bus) are never listened to, and a message identical to one just sent that arrives on any input within echoWindow milliseconds (default 40; 0 turns it off) is dropped as echo, once per message sent. midi.echoDropped counts them. To make an external program follow the show, ScoreMidi sends the score's segment changes and cues as notes and CCs (Score to MIDI).

modules: { sound: true } adds Sound (@openav/sound) with the Tone.js engine. Browsers only start audio after a click, so the console shows 🔊 enable sound in the L4 · Output — sound panel, with an instrument picker under it. Once enabled, every midi/note/on and midi/note/off plays the chosen instrument, whatever sent it (a keyboard, the QWERTY piano, the simulated performer, a phone). Tone.js (15.0.4) is loaded from jsDelivr only when sound is enabled. jsCopy

Pick from the console, or from code: jsCopy Switching while you play releases the notes held on the old instrument, so nothing hangs. A sampler keeps the old sound playing until its files are in, and the picker shows the progress. Each switch also fires the pulse signal sound/instrument ({ id, name }). The picker's last choice is remembered per page and wins over the declared instrument on the next visit; remember: false turns that off. The instrument is a discrete choice. What you perform continuously stays a param: the engine's params join the show's params under sound/. sound/cutoff (100–8000 Hz, default 2500), sound/space (reverb wet, 0–1, default 0.3) and sound/volume (−36–0 dB, default −8) are shared by every instrument, so a knob, a hand or the score plays the filter the way it plays the visuals. An instrument may suggest starting values (the piano opens the filter to 8000 Hz) and add knobs of its own, which the console shows while it plays: the organ's sound/drawbars and sound/rotor, sound/attack and sound/vibrato on the strings, sound/vowel on the choir, sound/tremolo on the electric piano and the vibraphone. Automation and overrides always win over a suggested default. A sound/* value reaches the engine when it changes. To set one by hand, show.sound.set('volume', -20) holds it against the timeline, a knob and a re-sent reading until show.sound.release('volume') or ✕ (Who holds a value). The sustain pedal (midi/cc/64) holds every instrument's note-offs. Notes on MIDI channel 10 (the drum machine) are left to a drum engine.

A sound you can pick is one file: data plus a create(Tone, ctx) that returns noteOn, noteOff and dispose. Import it before createShow() and every picker lists it; nothing in packages/* changes. jsCopy A duplicate id throws unless you pass registerInstrument(def, { replace: true }). Optional fields: defaults (starting cutoff, space, volume), credit, gain (dB), transpose (semitones), fallback (an id to play if loading fails) and, on the returned object, ready (a Promise: the picker shows progress while you call ctx.onProgress(0..1)), set(key, value) and releaseAll(time). Mallet sounds can be pure data with modalInstrument({ id, name, partials, strike }). A synth preset is data as well, and becomes synth/<id>: jsCopy

An engine is a small object, so you can replace the whole thing: jsCopy The drum kit from @openav/drums is also an engine: drumEngine({ samples }) maps General MIDI drum notes to synthesized drums (or to your samples, { 36: 'kick.wav', … }) and has one param, kitVolume (−30–0 dB).
createShow() is a convenience. When you need your own layout or loop, assemble the parts by hand; this is roughly what it does: jsCopy

A show that outgrows one afternoon needs a structure that can grow. The score (@openav/score) writes a show down as segments with lengths, and the director runs the code that performs each segment. They are pure logic with no DOM, and createShow() wires them to the timeline, the console and the prompter for you.

A timeline written as a table of absolute seconds cannot grow. Make the second scene longer and every later scene, cue, curve and if (t > 466) in your code is now wrong, and you find them one rehearsal at a time. In a score you write only how long each segment is: jsCopy Every start, end, cue time, countdown and scene is computed from those lengths. Change noon to dur: 40 and everything after it moves by ten seconds while everything before it stays put. A second version of the show is a few lines of data, not a second timeline to keep in step.

A cut is one version of the show. It has an id, an optional title, and either segments or a base cut and a scale. cut fieldmeaning idunique among the cuts; no . titleshown in the cut picker segmentsthe list below, in playing order from, scalea derived cut: the cut named from with every length times scale (scale > 0). It can be derived again; the scales multiply startthe id of the segment the show opens on and reset returns to (default: the first) segment fieldmeaning idunique within the cut; no .. It is also the id of the module that performs it title, notewhat the desk and the prompter show durlength in seconds, greater than 0. The only time a segment has cuesnamed moments inside the segment: a ratio 0 ≤ r < 1 (a fraction of the segment) or { s: seconds } (seconds into it) actswhat the human operator does in this segment: an array of strings, shown on the desk and, large, on the prompter lingerseconds the segment's module keeps running after the segment ends (a decay, a tail). Default 0 holdplayback stops at the end of this segment and waits for the operator (Hold) modulethe name of the module that performs it, when that is not the segment's own id metaanything else the work hangs on a segment (a layer, a palette, an event window): an object the score does not read and hands back as segment.meta. Other fields the score does not know are kept in meta too; an explicit meta entry wins A derived cut scales dur, linger and { s } cues, so a cue stays in the same place in the music. The ratio cues did not need to move. meta is plain data to the score: it is copied one level deep when the cut is built (changing your source object afterwards changes nothing), a derived cut shares its base cut's meta, and a module reads it as ctx.segment.meta. Treat it as read-only. segment.meta is always an object, {} when there is none; a meta that is not an object is a ScoreError. A cut is checked when the score is built. Duplicate ids, a dur of 0 or below, a from that is not a cut, a scale of 0 or below, a cut derived from itself, a cue outside its segment, acts that are not strings: each throws a ScoreError that names the cut, the segment and the reason, and lists every problem at once. Nothing half-valid can reach the stage.

Automation curves are written once, against the cut they were derived from, and a derived cut stretches them. timeline.valueAt(key, t) reads the curve at score.baseTime(t), which is t / scale. On the short cut above, t = 20 reads the curve at 40. A cut that is not derived has scale 1 and nothing changes. If two cuts differ in structure and not just in length, do not share automation written in absolute seconds between them. Write it per segment instead: automation: { haze: { dusk: [[0, 0.2], [1, 0.9, 'ease']] } } (p is the progress through the segment). The timeline compiles it against each root cut's own segment lengths, a cut that lacks a segment skips it, and a derived cut stretches it as above (Lanes). Or drive the params from the segment modules (param()), where ctx.p already scales for free.

A cue is a named moment: cues: { peak: 0.5 } in segment noon makes noon.peak, half way through. Three places see it: the scrubber draws a tick for it, and a click on the tick jumps there; the director calls onCue({ name, cue, T, n, segment }) once each time the playhead passes it while playing, and calls the active module's cue(name, ctx) hook; ctx.cue('peak') inside a module tells you where it sits, as a progress you can compare with ctx.p ('noon.peak' works for another segment's cue, ctx.cueT(name) answers in show seconds). A seek does not pass the cues it jumps over, and playing back over a cue fires it again. A cue sitting exactly on the first instant of the show fires on the first frame.

hold: true means: when playback reaches the end of this segment, stop and wait. A standby that waits for the room to be ready is the typical use. Exactly what happens: The timeline stops a microsecond before the boundary, so the show is still inside the held segment, and sets timeline.holding = true and timeline.playing = false. The clock freezes there for as long as you like. The held segment's module keeps getting update() every frame, with ctx.p === 1, ctx.holding === true and ctx.held, the number of seconds waited so far. Use ctx.held as the clock for anything that should keep breathing while the show is frozen. (This is the choice made: the show stops at the end of the segment rather than looping inside it. Looping would send p back to 0, fire the cues again and break "every module enters once, exits once".) Space, →, the ▶ button, timeline.play() and timeline.next() all release it: the next segment starts at once and playback continues. timeline.release() does the same in code. A seek (scrubber, goto, ←) or a reset clears the hold, and a seek never stops at a hold: only playback does. The last segment never holds (the show ends there). The backstage monitor shows ⏸ HOLD; the desk and the prompter show a pulsing banner.

A segment module is the code that performs one segment. Its id is the id of the segment (or the segment's module name): jsCopy enter, update and exit get the api object first (yours, see below). Every hook gets a ctx: ctxmeaning pprogress through the segment, 0 to 1. Above 1 during linger; exactly 1 while holding tseconds into the segment (p × dur) dtseconds since the previous frame durthe segment's length in seconds Tshow time in seconds segmentthe segment: id, title, start, end, dur, cues, acts, hold, linger, index, meta cue(name), cueT(name)where a cue sits, as a progress and in show seconds (NaN when unknown) phase'active', 'linger', or 'failed' (only inside exit() after a crash) holding, heldwaiting at a hold, and for how many seconds playingwhether the timeline is running (update is called every frame regardless) apithe same api object, so param() and cue() can reach the show too Enter once, exit once. The module of a segment is entered when the show enters it and exited when it leaves it, however it got there. A seek into the middle of a segment calls enter with the right p, so the module must be able to start from the middle. linger. After the segment ends its module keeps getting update() (with p > 1 and phase: 'linger') until the linger is over, and only then exit(). The next segment's module is already running meanwhile. param(). While a segment (or its linger) is current its module may rewrite any timeline param. Return a number to replace the value, anything else leaves it. The performer's hand still wins: an override is applied after this layer. A module that throws is switched off, alone. Each hook runs inside its own try/catch. If one throws, the director calls that module's exit() once (with phase: 'failed'), prints one console.error, and never calls it again. The other modules and the show carry on. The desk shows a red warning with the module's name and the error; R (reset) switches it back on. A frame loop is not allowed to stop because the youngest code in the room failed.

With a score the console adds: Scrubber. Segment blocks, a tick for every cue (click to jump) and a dashed end on a segment that holds. Curves panel (C). The automation of every param across the whole show, with the segment ids and the holds behind it, the playhead on each curve, and ↩ where a knob has taken a param away from its curve: The curves panel. Director panel. A cut picker (choosing one reloads the page with ?cut=<id>, so nothing is half-switched), the current segment with a progress bar and the time left, the HOLD banner, the next segment and the countdown, the operator's acts, this segment's cues (ticked as they pass), and the red warning for modules that were switched off. Prompter (T). Fullscreen, large, high-contrast: the segment title, what you do (acts), seconds left, the next segment, a HOLD banner while the show waits, and a red line for switched-off modules. Click it or press T again to leave. It also works for plain timeline scenes that carry acts.

keydoes Spaceplay / pause. At a HOLD: release it →next segment. At a HOLD: release it ←previous segment Rback to the start; stopped; switched-off modules come back Tprompter Ffullscreen Ccurves panel Escstop the knob-mapping wizard, or leave keyboard-piano capture Typing in a field, a held key (auto-repeat) and any key with ⌘, Ctrl or Alt are ignored. While the on-screen piano captures the keyboard (the keyboard box ticked in the piano bar) the letters belong to the piano: R, T, F and C do nothing, because T and F are piano keys, and an accidental R must not rewind a show you are playing. Space, the arrows and Esc always work, so you can play and run the show from one keyboard. The MIDI-controller key M follows the same rule.

The L2 Mapping panel has 🎛 map knobs in order. It arms learn for the first param, you turn one knob, it is bound and the next param is armed; skip, back and stop (or Esc) steer it. Learn only ever adds routes (Mapper.learn), so running it again puts a second knob on a param and keeps the first. The order is the declared order of the params, skipping hidden ones; pass mountConsole(el, app, { learnOrder: ['hue', 'size'] }) for your own. The logic is LearnWizard in @openav/mapping: jsCopy

Software that should follow the show (a DAW launching a clip per segment, a lighting desk jumping scenes) cannot read the score, but it can read MIDI. ScoreMidi (@openav/midi) turns segment changes and cues into notes and CCs. It is off unless you ask: jsCopy optiondefaultmeaning channel15MIDI channel 1 to 16 segment{ note: 36 }note: base note, the note sent is note + index. cc: a CC whose value is the index. velocity. false turns segment markers off cue{ note: 84 }note for every cue, notes: { 'seg.name': note } for particular ones, cc whose value is the cue's number in the cut. false turns cue markers off length0.15seconds before a marker note's note-off scrubfalsealso mark when the playhead is moved by hand. By default markers go out only while the show plays (or a hold is released), so dragging the scrubber does not launch clips A reset never sends. Everything goes through the Midi engine's own noteOn/cc, so the MIDI OUT meter shows it and panic() silences it. In code: new ScoreMidi({ midi, channel, segment, cue }), then .segment({ index, cause }) and .cue({ name, n }).

A show that keeps two time lines (a story time that old logic reads and a show time the audience lives) needs a way to say which engine follows which: weather that never stops, a city that pauses while an inserted segment plays. That is a clock per engine. This framework has one time line, the show's T, so there is nothing for a clock to choose between, and a segment module that wants to pause an engine simply stops advancing it (ctx.t is its own clock, ctx.held another). If a real show brings back the two-time-line case, a clocks table belongs in the cut next to segments. Until then it would be machinery with no user.
