DMX512 is how stage lights are told what to do: one cable carries a universe of 512 channels, each a number from 0 to 255, sent about 40 times a second. A light listens to a few channels starting at its address (a par might read dimmer, red, green, blue, white, strobe from address 1 to 6), and what each channel means is in its manual, its profile. Networks carry many universes at once (Art-Net, sACN), and a USB interface turns a computer's numbers into the cable's signal. @openav/dmx puts a lighting rig inside a work: fixture profiles, a patch, an engine that renders every light at any moment from scenes, cues, chases and effects, and three ways to get the bytes out. It runs with no light and no interface: the monitor on the page shows what the rig is getting. Example 28 is all of it in one page. Warning Nothing here has been tried with a real fixture, node or interface yet. The bytes follow the published layouts of Art-Net 4, ANSI E1.31 and the Enttec DMX USB Pro API, and the tests decode every packet on this machine, but no light has received them for this project. Before a show, check your rig with the section Check it in TouchDesigner and with the lights themselves, and keep a hand on blackout.

wayfromwhat you needgood for out-bridge + Art-Netthe page → ws://127.0.0.1:6450/out → UDP 6454node packages/out/bridge/out-bridge.mjs --config out.json, an Art-Net nodevenues, most network nodes, many universes out-bridge + sACNthe page → the bridge → UDP 5568 (multicast or unicast)the same bridge, an sACN (E1.31) receiverconsoles and newer nodes, priority between sources Web Serial + Enttec DMX USB Prothe page → USB, no bridgeChrome or Edge on a computer, a DMX USB Pro or an interface that speaks its protocolone interface, one universe, a classroom A browser cannot send UDP, so the network protocols leave through the out-bridge, the same local program that drives WLED strips and motor boards (@openav/out). The page sends one value per DMX address on channels named dmx/<universe>/<address>, and the bridge's artnet, sacn or enttec sink keeps a 512-byte buffer per universe and sends it at a fixed 40 Hz while it changes, and once a second while it does not (a node that hears nothing for about 2.5 s decides the source is gone). jsonCopy Art-Net goes to the node's address (host, or a list of them). Art-Net 4 says ArtDmx is never broadcast: 40 packets a second per universe would reach every device on the network and flood slow nodes and Wi-Fi. "broadcast": true is there for an old node that only listens to broadcast, on a network that carries nothing else. sACN goes to each universe's multicast group 239.255.<high byte>.<low byte> (receivers join the groups they want), or to host when you give one. priority is 0–200 (100 by default: a receiver takes the highest it hears), source is the name a console shows, interface picks the network card multicast leaves from. A clean stop sends three "stream terminated" packets after the safe values. Enttec writes one universe to a DMX USB Pro on a serial device. A missing device is a status, retried every 2 s, never a crash. Web Serial needs no bridge: dmxTransport('serial') and a Connect button (the browser asks which port, only from a click). Chrome and Edge on a computer only, on https or localhost. Not here: an Enttec Open DMX or any bare FTDI cable (the computer would have to time the DMX break itself, which a page cannot do reliably), RDM, Art-Net discovery (ArtPoll), ArtSync.

"Universe 1" is the number you patch on and the number in the channel name, dmx/1/…. It leaves as Art-Net Port-Address 1 (Net 0, Sub-Net 0, Universe 1) and as sACN universe 1. dmx/N/… is Port-Address N (up to 32767, Net · Sub-Net · Universe in one 15-bit number) and sACN universe N (up to 63999). Some software calls its first universe "1" but sends it as Art-Net Port-Address 0, which Art-Net 4 deprecates. If a node is set to 0, patch the page on universe 0 (dmx/0/… reaches it through Art-Net; sACN has no universe 0) or, better, set the node to 1. encodeArtDmx() takes the Port-Address itself and defaults to 1.

A profile says which channels a light has and in which order each mode sends them. The generic ones ship with the package (FIXTURES: a dimmer, RGB, RGBW, RGBA and RGBAW+UV pars, a strobe, a moving head in 8 and 16 channels); a real fixture's profile is a JSON file you copy and change to match its manual. None of them is marked verified, because only a person with the light in front of them can say a profile is right. Forty-two real fixtures come from the Open Fixture Library (MIT), converted and kept out of FIXTURES (loadImportedFixture(id) from @openav/dmx/fixtures/imported.js, or device(id) of @openav/devices, loads the one you ask for). Every fixture, generic or imported, has a page at /fixtures/<id>/ with each mode's channel table, a virtual fixture to try and the code that patches it: the DMX fixtures of the device collection, for example the Chauvet DJ SlimPAR T12 BT. The patch puts fixtures on universes and addresses, in groups, with limits: jsCopy A work never names channel numbers. It asks for properties, each 0..1: dimmer, color: [r, g, b], pan, tilt, strobe, zoom. The patch turns them into each light's bytes: the colour is split into the emitters the fixture has (white first on an RGBW par), pan and tilt become two bytes where the mode has a fine channel, and a fixture with no dimmer channel gets the dimmer in its colour.

DmxEngine renders every light at any moment as a pure function of time: the same t always gives the same bytes, so a look can be checked with no light and a recording can be rendered frame by frame. The layers, bottom to top: layercallwhat it is basescene(name, { target: props }), base(...names)the look that is just on cuescue(name, { scene, fadeIn, fadeOut, curve }), go(name, at), release(at)go to a scene with a fade, as on a lighting desk chaseschase(name, { steps, every, unit, fade }), run(name, on)scenes in turn, every n beats or seconds effectseffect(name, { target, property, wave, rate, depth, spread }), tune(name, { rate, depth }, at)sine, saw, square, chase, flicker or rainbow over a group, each fixture a little behind the one before live valuesset(target, props)a fader, the microphone: on top of everything submasterssubmaster(target, level)a fader over a group: scales the dimmer of what every layer made lastengine.master, engine.blackout, the patch's limitsgrand master, blackout, per-fixture limits A target is a fixture id, a group, '*' or a list of them. tune() changes a running effect's rate without a jump: the wave goes on from where it is, only faster or slower. (Defining the effect again would restart its phase, and a knob turned on a wave that is 100 seconds along would sweep it through many cycles at once.) jsCopy

dmxTransport() takes what render() returns, every frame, and delivers only what changed: jsCopy Every transport puts the frame through the flash guard before anything leaves (see Safety); { patch } lets it read each fixture's light. The bridge transport calls client.set('dmx/<universe>/<address>', byte / 255) once per changed channel. The serial one writes a whole Enttec frame (all 512 channels) when anything in its universe changed, at most one every 25 ms, and once a second otherwise. In a lab work, "modules": ["out", "dmx"] gives lab.dmx: a patch from meta.dmx.patch, its engine, the transport with the flash guard on (?dmx=bridge goes through lab.out, ?dmx=serial to an Enttec Pro), lab.dmx.frame(t) to render and send, lab.dmx.monitor(el) and lab.dmx.params(options).

The engine never reads a signal (the framework's first rule: continuous control goes through params). dmxParams() turns its control points into params, and from then on the lights are performed like any world: jsCopy keydrives dmx/masterthe grand master dmx/blackoutblackout (a step param, 0 or 1) dmx/<group>/dimmera submaster over the group: cues, chases and effects keep running under it dmx/<group>/hue, /saturationthe group's colour, in a base scene of its own (a rainbow effect mixes over it) dmx/<effect>/rate, /depththe effect, through tune(): no jump when a knob moves dmx/<chase>/runa chase on or off Now the mapper connects anything to them, in routes or with learn in the L2 · Mapping panel: jsCopy The timeline automates the same keys (automation: { 'dmx/pars/hue': [[0, 0.07], [24, 0.58]] }), a phone surface shows them as faders (their group is lights), and a world's own params can feed both the picture and the lights.

Blackout. engine.blackout = true (or the dmx/blackout param, or the Blackout button in example 28) takes every dimmer to 0 at once (and the colour of a fixture that has no dimmer channel, since its dimmer is in its colour), and leaves pan, tilt, zoom and control channels where they are, so a moving head does not swing when the room goes dark. Limits. Each placed fixture can have limits ({ dimmer: [0, 0.8], tilt: [0.1, 0.9] }), applied after every layer, before the grand master. Flashing, per fixture. Flashing faster than about three times a second can bring on a seizure in people with photosensitive epilepsy. What matters is the light one fixture really gives, so the cap, maxFlashHz (3 by default), is held per fixture, in two layers. In the engine. Each effect and each chase is first held to the cap on its own: a rate in seconds is clamped, a rate in beats is halved until it fits (so it stays on the beat), a chase's step is doubled, a random flicker draws no more new values than that. Then, for each fixture, the rates of everything that flashes it (effects on its dimmer or colour, chases that change it with anything but position) are added up. When the sum is over the cap, those sources are slowed on that fixture until it is not: a rate in seconds by the same factor, a rate in beats halved, a chase's step doubled. Two 3 Hz effects on one par run at 1.5 Hz each there, and on the pars that carry only one of them they keep their speed. engine.state(t).slowed (and describe().slowed) lists the fixtures slowed, with their sum before and after and each source. This layer is still a pure function of time: the same t gives the same bytes, so a recording renders frame by frame as before. tune() keeps every wave on a shared fixture going from where it is when a knob changes one of them. At the output. Every dmxTransport() (sim, bridge and serial) puts the frame through a flash guard before it leaves. It reads each fixture's brightness from the bytes (its intensity times its brightest colour channel) and counts a flash the way WCAG 2.3.1 does: a pair of opposing changes of 10% of full scale or more, measured from the last turning point. No fixture may brighten by that much more than 3 times in any second: when the next rise would be one too many, the light stays at the level it last had, steady, until the second has room. Falls always pass, so blackout and a cue to dark land on the next frame, and the guard never sends more light than was asked. It holds only the intensity bytes (the colour bytes, scaled together, on a fixture with no dimmer channel); pan, tilt,…

dmxTransport('sim', { patch }) keeps the bytes in memory, after the flash guard; out.bytes(1) is universe 1, out.changed the channels of the last send. mountDmxMonitor(el, { patch, transport, engine }) draws the rig on the page: one swatch per fixture (its colour times its dimmer, a moving head's pan and tilt as a small mark) and the 512 channels of a universe as a grid, each cell its value as a bar, tinted by what it drives. Point at a cell to read its address, value, fixture and channel. Everything is read back from the bytes, so a profile one channel off shows the wrong colour here too. monitor.update() with no argument shows what the transport delivered, after the flash guard; the header says what the guard is doing, held fixtures get an amber ring, and with the engine the fixtures its per-fixture cap slows are marked "slow". Example 28 draws a stage with the same lights and the monitor under it, on the sim transport by default: ?out=bridge sends to the out-bridge, ?out=serial adds a Connect button for an Enttec Pro. tests/dmx-out.test.js runs the bridge on this machine and decodes every Art-Net and sACN packet it sends with the package's own decoders.

TouchDesigner's DMX In CHOP is a second receiver that has nothing to do with this code, which makes it a good check before a rig is in the room. In out.json, send universe 1 to this machine: { "match": "dmx/1/*", "sink": "artnet", "host": "127.0.0.1" } (or "sink": "sacn", "host": "127.0.0.1"). Start the bridge. In TouchDesigner, add a DMX In CHOP. For Art-Net, pick the Art-Net interface and set Net 0, Subnet 0, Universe 1 (Port-Address 1). For sACN, pick sACN and universe 1. Open example 28 with ?out=bridge. The CHOP shows 512 channels moving: par 1 is channels 1 to 6 (dimmer, red, green, blue, white, strobe), head 1 starts at 49. Close the tab: within half a second the channels go to their safe values. This check has not been run for this project yet, and the CHOP's parameter names may read a little differently in your version of TouchDesigner.

What was checked: the byte layouts against the specifications, every packet decoded on this machine (universe, bytes, at most 44 packets a second, the keep-alive, safe values when the page goes away), the Enttec sink and the Web Serial transport against stand-in ports, the engine's caps and fades and both flash layers in npm test (flashes counted at 40 frames a second on injected clocks, by a counter written apart from the guard), and example 28 in a headless browser with no permission for serial or MIDI. The flash guard has not been watched on a real light: what a fixture does with a held intensity byte (its own dimmer curve, its fade time) is not known here. What was not: a real Art-Net node, an sACN receiver or console, an Enttec DMX USB Pro, any real fixture's channels, and TouchDesigner as a receiver. If you have any of them, try it and tell us what you saw.

The stage on a projector, a second screen, OBS or TouchDesigner. @openav/output (since 0.12.0) opens an output window that shows the stage, bends it so a projector that is not square to the wall still lands as a rectangle (corner-pin), crops one canvas for several projectors side by side, and gives each output a blackout and a brightness that are params. Any show also has a clean address, ?output: the same page with the stage alone on black, for a kiosk browser, OBS's Browser Source or TouchDesigner's Web Render TOP. The world never knows any of this happened. Example 29, Projector output runs all of it on one screen. This is one stage, rendered once and shown through output windows. Phones, tablets and laptops lying on a table, each drawing its own part of one canvas from where a photo says it lies, are Several screens, one canvas (@openav/tile): its homography() takes any number of measured points, where cornerPin() here is the four corners of one window. A wall of several outputs aligned from one layout file, with a mesh, feathered edges and masks per projector, is Projector and LED alignment (@openav/align): the four-corner part of its calibration imports into these windows (createOutputs(show, { align })).

Declare the outputs once, at load, and open one from a click (a browser opens a window only after a gesture): jsCopy createOutputs adds the params output/main/blackout and output/main/brightness at once, boxes the stage on this page to 16:9 (centred, black around it) so the world draws the shape the projector has, and puts an L4 · Output panel on the desk: per output Open (a mirror window), Page (a second page, below), Edit and Grid, whether it is open and how large, and Export layout, Import layout and Lead. openOutput(show, { name }) does the same for one output without the declaration (its params appear when it opens). The window is black, has no console, and hides the cursor after two seconds. Its keys: keywhat it does Ffullscreen (again: leave it) Eedit the corners (below); E or Esc again when done Gthe test pattern: a grid, a crosshair, circles, the four edges in colour (top red, right green, bottom blue, left yellow) Bblackout on or off: it writes the param output/<name>/blackout, so the desk shows it and ✕ clears it Ithe help card These keys belong to the output window. The show's own keys (Space, the arrows, R) do not see them, and the output window's keys never move the show.

Measured in headless Chromium 151 (software rendering): the video has the canvas's exact size, and the centres of eight flat colour blocks read back exactly as drawn. Fine detail (where a stream with less colour resolution would show) and a GPU-backed Chrome were not measured. Page is the one for a second machine, for an output larger than the operator's canvas, or for a world that is not a canvas. outputs.open('main', { mode: 'page' }), or the Page button.

On one screen the output is just a window: press F in it. With a projector or a second screen, drag the window onto it and press F. Where the browser has the Window Management API (window.getScreenDetails, Chromium) and the computer reports more than one screen, the window's card also offers Find the screens…: the browser asks once whether this site may place windows on all your screens, then lists them (label · width×height), and a click on one goes fullscreen on that screen with requestFullscreen({ screen }). The permission is only ever asked from a click inside the output window, never on its own, and when it was granted before, the screens are listed without asking. When it is refused, or the API is not there (Safari, Firefox), the card says what always works: drag the window, press F. (MDN: Window Management API, Element.requestFullscreen: fullscreen needs a user gesture, which is why every fullscreen here is a key or a click in the output window itself.)

A projector that is not square to the wall throws a trapezoid. Press E in the output window and drag its four numbered handles onto the corners of the screen (or of the wall area you want): the picture bends so that it lands as a rectangle. Pick a corner with 1 to 4 (or Tab) and move it with the arrows, 1 px at a time, Shift for 10 px. Turn the test pattern on (G) while you do it: its grid shows straight lines and even cells when the corners are right. key (editing) drag a handle, or 1–4 / Tab and the arrowsmove a corner (Shift ×10) H, Vmirror left–right (rear projection), top–bottom (a projector hung upside down that cannot flip itself) O, Shift+Oturn the picture 90° clockwise, back (a projector on its side) [ ]a black border, 0.5 % of each side at a time, up to 45 % (overscan: bring back edges that fall off the screen) R, Shift+Rthe corners back to the window's; everything back Four points decide one projective transform (a homography). cornerPin(corners, width, height) computes it and toMatrix3d() writes it as a CSS matrix3d(…), so the browser bends the whole output, picture and test pattern together, on the GPU, with nothing redrawn. A quad no projector can throw (a corner pushed inside, two edges crossed, three corners on a line) is refused: the corner stays where it was. A soft edge (soft, from 0 to 0.5) fades the picture's edges to black over that share of each side; it is a fade, not edge blending.

Every change is saved in this browser under oav-output:<name>, so the venue's setup survives a reload, and a clean page of the same name in the same browser uses it too. Export layout writes every output's room to a file you can carry to the next rehearsal, and Import layout checks one, saves it and applies it to open windows: jsonCopy The file is the room, the code is the show: it holds what the venue did to each output (corners as 0..1 of the output window, flips, turn, border, soft edge), never what the output shows. Crops live in the code. parseOutputLayout() refuses a file with one message that lists every problem (outputs.main.rotate: must be 0, 90, 180 or 270), so a file is fixed in one go.

Rule 1: what is performed goes through params. Each output has two, declared before any window opens: paramrange output/<name>/blackout0 or 11: this output is black, whatever it shows output/<name>/brightness0 to 1, default 1a black veil over the picture (1 - brightness of it); not the projector's lamp So the console's sliders, a MIDI fader, the timeline and a phone all reach the projector the same way they reach the world. Example 29 fades the projector out over the last 8 seconds of its timeline and gives it to any controller's volume fader: jsCopy

One wide canvas, two projectors side by side: declare two outputs, each with its crop of the stage ({ x, y, w, h }, 0 to 1), and give the stage the shape of both together. jsCopy Each output has its own corners, its own params and its own window (open each from its own click: a browser opens one window per gesture). fit says how a crop fills its window when the shapes differ: contain (default, black bars), cover (filled, cut) or stretch. Example 29 does this with ?pair. Where the two pictures meet there is a hard seam: edge blending (two projectors overlapping with a matched soft ramp and brightness) is not part of this package: @openav/align feathers the overlap in WebGL (Projector and LED alignment).

Every page built with createShow() becomes a clean output when its address says so. The desk, the piano, the hints, the MIDI button, the phone card, the example guide, and anything a show marks with the class oav-operator, are not shown, and the desk's keys are off. The stage fills the window on black, with the corners this browser saved for that output name and the same keys as an output window (E, G, F, B, I). For a page to follow, the show page has to lead: Lead on the panel, outputs.lead() in code, or example 29 opened with ?lead. Across browsers (OBS and TouchDesigner each run their own) or machines that needs the relay: run node serve.js on the show machine and use via=relay. A clean page that does not follow runs the show by itself: its timeline plays only with &play, and its inputs are whatever the show declares, with nobody at them. A clean page that follows takes no input (keyboard piano, MIDI, microphone, camera, phones are off) and shows what the show page's clock and held values say; a note played on the show page does not reach it. To carry live playing exactly, mirror (above) or capture the show page's window (OBS, below).

What was checked: the output window, its keys, the corner-pin, the layout surviving a reload, the clean address, in headless Chromium 151 on one machine. Not yet: a real projector, a second physical screen, and the screen picker's permission prompt. Run the show from this machine: node serve.js, then open http://localhost:8080/examples/29-projector-output/ (or your show) in Chrome. Connect the projector and set the computer to extend the desktop onto it (not mirror the display). Click Open output window. Drag the window onto the projector and press F in it (or Find the screens… and click the projector). Press G, then E. Drag the four corners onto the screen's corners until the grid's cells look even. Press E to finish. Press G again to see the show. The layout is saved: a reload, and the window opened again, land in the same place. Export layout and keep the file with the show: the next rehearsal in this room imports it. Before the audience comes in: try B (blackout) and its fader, and the end of the timeline. For a machine that only shows the picture (a kiosk), open the clean address in Chrome's kiosk mode. --kiosk is "Enable kiosk mode" (not Chrome OS kiosk mode), --autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required lets the page's sound start without a click, and --user-data-dir is the folder where the browser keeps all of its state, so a folder of its own keeps the kiosk's saved corners and permissions apart from your everyday profile: bashCopy The switches come from the Chromium switch list (peter.sh) and the autoplay flag from Chrome's autoplay policy ("Muted autoplay is always allowed"; the flag lifts the gesture rule for sound). A kiosk window opens on the screen Chrome chooses: which one, and whether --start-fullscreen or --window-position move it to the projector, is to be confirmed on the venue machine. Corners for a kiosk profile are set in that profile: open the clean address there once without --kiosk, press E, or import the layout file on a normal page of that profile. The venue checklist, beyond the pre-show checklist: the display is extended, the projector's own keystone is off or at zero (correct in one place only), its resolution is native the computer does not sleep, dim or show notifications; the projector's own sleep is off the show runs from this machine (node serve.js), not from the internet: no network needed during the show the layout file exported, and tried on a reload blackout tested from the desk, from its fader, and with B in the output window what happens when the show page reloads: open the output again (mirror), or nothing to do…

Where they sit in OBS's menus is to be confirmed with the plugin installed. Window capture instead. To send exactly what the performer plays (notes, particles, the mirror), capture the window rather than load the page again: macOS Screen Capture (or Window Capture), pointed at the output window. The output window has no console and hides its cursor, so the capture is clean; keep it on a screen (a hidden window may not be drawn), and crop with the source's Crop if needed.

Headless Chromium 151 (Playwright 1.62), one machine, node serve.js, no permissions granted (no MIDI, serial, camera, microphone or window management): example 29 loads with no console errors (the ws://…7457 monitor warning is expected), its stage boxed to 16:9 Open output window opens the window; the video has the canvas's exact size and its frames advance; the centres of eight flat colour blocks read back as drawn. A mirror of example 06 (a p5.js WEBGL canvas) shows its picture too: the world needed nothing E shows four handles; dragging two corners and nudging a third with the keys changes the window's matrix3d and saves exactly those corners; G shows the test pattern; B writes output/main/blackout and the veil goes black; brightness 0.4 from the desk gives a veil of 0.6; the output window's keys never moved the show after a reload of the show page, the output opens again in the same window with the same corners, and plays Page opens the clean address as a follower over a BroadcastChannel; a page in a second, separate browser context at ?output&follow=oav-output&via=relay follows example 29 opened with ?lead over node serve.js's relay. Both hold the show page's blackout and a slider it moved, and their own measure of the error (timeline.followStatus().error) stayed under 3 ms and under 8 ms over a second the clean address shows no desk, piano, hint, guide or operator button, and uses the saved corners; ?pair&output=left draws the 32:9 stage at twice the window's width and shows its left half every example built with createShow() (01 to 09, 12 to 14, 27 to 29) still starts with no console errors, and 01, 05, 06, 07, 13 and 14 at ?output show the stage alone filling the window, with no errors, the artwork credit of 05, 06 and 07 still on it Not checked: a real projector, a second physical screen, the Window Management permission prompt and fullscreen on a chosen screen, a browser's popup blocker (the test browser runs without one; a window opens from a click by the browsers' rule), Chrome's kiosk mode, TouchDesigner, OBS, NDI.

Phones, tablets and laptops lying flat on a table, of any size, turned any way, partly on top of each other, become one canvas. @openav/tile covers each screen with small markers, finds them all in one photo taken from above, and from then on every screen draws only its own piece of one shared picture. A dot that leaves one screen travels behind the bezel and comes out on the next one where it would really be, at the same size. Nothing is streamed: every screen computes its own frame from the same two things, one clock shared through the relay and one seed. Example 30, Tile dot is one dot and its sparks flowing across every screen. This is not the projector chapter. Projection and video out is one stage, rendered once, shown through output windows on projectors and second screens. Here many devices each render their own part of one canvas, placed by a photo. The two can meet in one show, but neither needs the other. A wall of projectors or LED outputs aligned from one layout file, by hand, is a third thing: Projector and LED alignment.

You need a computer on the same wifi as the phones (it runs the relay), three screens to tile and one more phone to take the photo (it can be one of the three, in a second tab, before you lay it down). On the computer, in the repository: node serve.js. It prints the address phones can reach, for example http://192.168.1.20:8080. On each screen open http://192.168.1.20:8080/examples/30-tile-dot/?room=desk and tap Tap to join (fullscreen, and keep the screen awake). Lay the screens flat: any angle, any spacing, overlapping is fine. On the camera phone open http://192.168.1.20:8080/packages/tile/?room=desk. Every screen appears in the list within a second, with its number, its pixels, and whether it is fullscreen and awake. Press Markers: every screen turns white with black markers. Press Take photo and photograph the table from above with every screen in the frame. Each screen needs at least four markers in view; a hand or another phone over the rest is fine. Straight down is best, up to about 45° works. The camera page outlines what it found on the photo and draws a plan of the canvas. When every screen was placed it sends the layout and presses Play: the dot starts flowing. A screen that was missed says why in the list (too-few-markers, …): take the photo again, or press Play anyway. Moved a screen? Markers, then a photo again. A screen that reloads keeps its place (its layout is kept on the device and replayed by the relay) as long as its size did not change. No screens at hand: packages/tile/?demo=1 runs the same detection and solve on a synthetic photo of three screens under a tilted camera and compares the result with the truth. The page of example 30 without ?room= is one screen on its own, with the console, on its own time.

packages/tile/?room=<name> joins the room as its runner. It hears every screen's hello, gives each a number (its markers, 0 to 19, remembered for that room), and answers with standing config the relay replays to a screen that joins later: the numbers, Markers or Play, the layout, and the show's seed and start. New start + seed starts every screen again together, and layout.json downloads the last layout. Take photo (<input capture>) opens the phone's camera app at its full resolution and works on any address. Live camera (getUserMedia, one frame) needs a secure context, so it works on localhost or https://, not on http://192.168…. A photo larger than 4096 pixels on its long side is scaled down before detection. The markers are found by OpenCV.js's ArUco detector (@techstark/opencv-js@4.12.0-release.1, a plain build of OpenCV 4.12.0, from jsDelivr, pinned). It is about 10 MB (3 MB over the wire), loaded by the camera page only and only when the first photo comes in, then cached. The screens never load it: the bits of their markers are in dict.js, extracted from OpenCV (see NOTICE), and no other page or package of the framework refers to it (tests/tile.test.js checks). A venue without the internet can serve its own copy of that file and pass it to loadOpenCV(url).

Wrap the world, route the camera page's mode to the marker param, keep the timeline on the shared clock, and draw in canvas units through the view: jsCopy Time. Read io.tile.time() (shared seconds) and io.tile.seed. Two screens that started a second apart, or one that dropped a frame, must still draw the same instant, so positions are functions of time and seed, never sums of dt (example 30 samples its dot's tail back in time instead of remembering past frames). This is the one place a tiled world reads a clock, and it is the shared one. Params stay the world's continuous controls (rule 1). tileMarkers is a param like any other: the camera page drives it through tile/markers, and the timeline or a knob can too. It follows the rule for who holds a value: a slider moved by hand on one screen's console holds that screen until the camera page really changes mode. The view. view.apply2d(ctx, pixelRatio) for a 2D canvas, view.applyP5(sk) at the top of a p5 draw(), transform: view.css(devicePixelRatio) with transform-origin: 0 0 for an element. view.visible(x, y, r) skips what is not on this screen, view.scale is device pixels per canvas unit. The canvas is measured in the reference screen's pixels and includes the gaps and bezels.

Every screen pings the relay ten times when it connects and then every 2 s. The relay already answers every ping with its own time; ClockSync keeps the offset of the quickest round trip of the last minute (NTP, simplified: the error is at most half that round trip, a few ms on home wifi). tile.now() is the relay's clock read on this screen, and tile.time() the seconds since the camera page pressed Play. Screens refresh on their own vsync, so two of them can still be a frame apart. syncTimeline(timeline, dt), called before timeline.advance(dt) (createShow's onFrame is), puts the playhead where the shared clock was one frame ago, so the frame lands on the shared time and fires the scenes and cues it passes; the automation then reads the same values on every screen. The shared clock never waits, so neither does a tiled timeline: a pause or a seek on one screen is undone on the next frame, and a hold scene parks it for one frame and is then released (the next scene starts and its boundary cue fires). This is not @openav/sync, and the two are kept apart on purpose: @openav/syncthe tile clock who keeps timeone leader page runs the timeline and says every frame where it isnobody: every screen asks the relay what time it is what travelsthe leader's playhead (T, playing, holding, rate, cut) every frame, and extra datanothing per frame: each screen's hello once a second and a ping every 2 s; the layout and the start once, as config pause, hold, seekcopied by every followernot shared: undone on the next frame, a hold released when a page drops outa follower that loses the leader runs on by itself (timeline.follow())the camera page can close: the screens play on forseveral pages of one show at their own sizes: a wall of outputs, a lobby, a rehearsal laptopone canvas cut into pieces, every piece drawn from (time, seed) Nothing in the framework joins the two, and they have not been tried together on one page.

Every screen lies in one plane, the table, and its pixels are evenly spaced on it, so "screen pixels → table" is a similarity (a turn, a uniform scale, a shift) for every screen, whatever its pixel density. The camera adds one perspective, "table → photo", the same for all of them. So each screen's homography H_i (screen pixels → photo) is G · S_i, and H_ref⁻¹ · H_i = S_ref⁻¹ · S_i is a similarity: the camera's perspective cancels, and a phone's 460 ppi against a laptop's 227 ppi ends up in the scale. solveLayout(): per screen, a normalized DLT homography from all its marker corners. A marker whose corners land far from it is dropped once (a misread id). Fewer than 4 markers: the screen is reported as too-few-markers, not solved, and nothing throws; the reference is the screen that covers the most of the photo; each other screen's similarity is a least-squares fit of its own corners to its photo corners taken back through H_ref⁻¹; one plane G and every S_i are refined together by Levenberg–Marquardt, so the perspective is measured by every marker on the table (it keeps a screen far from the reference right); the canvas is moved so the union of the screens starts at (0, 0). Each screen carries 50 markers of DICT_5X5_1000 (id = screen × 50 + cell, so up to 20 screens), four across its short side. Five by five, not four by four: two of these markers differ in at least 5 bits under rotation, and a misread id puts four corners on the wrong screen. The result, layout.json: jsonCopy similarity maps a screen's pixel to the canvas, matrix3x3 is the same matrix row by row, rms the reprojection error in photo pixels; validateLayout() lists every problem of a file, one message each. A device of "kind": "window" with a "pose" is the room kept for the next step, a screen posed in 3D (a laptop standing up, a screen on a wall, a projector): this version validates it and its view says it cannot draw it yet.

A tile is a controller in a relay room and the camera page is its runner; the hub in packages/relay is unchanged. fromnamewhat tilesignal tile/<id>/hello{ id, w, h, dpr, screen, css, fullscreen, wake }, re-sent every second cameraconfig tile/roster{ grid, devices: [{ id, index, w, h }] }: each screen's number cameraconfig tile/mode'markers' or 'show' cameraconfig tile/layoutlayout.json cameraconfig tile/show{ seed, start }: the start on the shared clock Into the show's signals: tile/markers (0 or 1, the camera page's mode), tile/synced (0 or 1) and the pulse tile/layout. On a static host (openaudiovisual.com) there is no relay: run node serve.js, or point every page at one with ?relay=wss://…. The relay has no authentication: use a closed network and a room name nobody will guess (Security).

iPhone Safari cannot make a page fullscreen. Add the page to the home screen and open it from there. Without fullscreen it still works, but the browser bars become part of the bezel and change size when they hide, which unplaces the screen until the next photo. Keeping the screen on is the system setting's job (iPhone: Auto-Lock, Never; Android: Screen timeout). The wake lock is a backup: it needs the tap, the system drops it when the page is hidden (the ⛶ button asks again), and browsers offer it only on https:// or localhost (on http://192.168… the camera page lists it as n/a). Flat screens only. A laptop standing up does not lie in the table's plane: lay it flat or wait for the 3D model. Overlapping screens: which one is on top is not known, so the one underneath also draws the part that is covered. A screen that changes size (a rotation, the address bar) draws on its own until the next photo. A param moved by hand on one screen's console changes that screen only; what is shared is the timeline, the clock and the seed. The timeline cannot be paused or held on a tile: it follows the shared clock. Up to 20 screens. Glossy screens reflect lamps: turn the brightness up and avoid a light right above the table. Two tabs of one browser share an id (it is kept in localStorage): add &id=a, &id=b when trying it on one computer.

On one machine, with no screens but browser contexts and no hardware at all: tests/tile.test.js (in npm test): the DLT and the similarity fit against known transforms with 0.5 px of noise; the solve on synthetic photos (a pinhole camera, real screen sizes and densities) for two and three screens, with 4 markers and with fewer, a misread marker, with and without the refinement; a dot crossing screens stays continuous; layout.json validation; marker ids, the grid and the dictionary; the view's matrices; the clock; syncTimeline through scenes, a cue, a hold scene, a pause and a seek; the tileMarkers route under the rule for who holds a value; and that only the camera page can reach OpenCV. packages/tile/test/tile-smoke.cjs, by hand, in headless Chromium with the pinned OpenCV.js from jsDelivr: example 30 alone with no console errors; the camera page's ?demo=1 placing its three synthetic screens within 0.2°, 0.5 % and 2 px of the truth; then a live room over node serve.js of three tile pages the size of a laptop, a tablet and a phone, whose own screenshots make the photo the camera page detects and solves: every tile placed within 1 mm of where it lies, the dot continuous across them, their clocks and their timelines agreeing. Never tried yet: phones and tablets on a real table, a real photo (reflections, light, the angle, a phone small in the frame), fullscreen and the wake lock on an iPhone or an Android phone, the clock over a real wifi, and a 12 MP photo's detection time on a phone. The README of the package lists what to look at when it is.

A wall made of several outputs, two projectors side by side with a blend band, an LED band folded into two 4K ports, a room corner on a splitter, is written once, as one JSON file: the layout. @openav/align (since 0.13.0) reads that file three ways: the test patterns, the vendor's alignment chart, and the real output mapping of the work. All three read the same data, so a pattern that is right on the wall means the work is right on the wall. On top of the layout goes a calibration made by hand on the venue day: four corners, a mesh, feathered edges, masks and brightness, for each projector. For the camera-in-the-loop alignment that will one day do this by itself, the package has the pattern generator, channel-separated Gray code. Nothing that reads a camera is built yet. Example 31, Align runs all of it on one screen with no hardware. This is not the projector window and not the tiling. Projection and video out is one stage shown through output windows, four corners each. Several screens, one canvas is many devices each drawing their own piece, placed by a photo. Output, tile and align says how the three differ and how align's calibration reaches an output window.

The art canvas is the wall unrolled flat: a curved wall or a room's walls side by side become one rectangle, and the work draws at that size. A segment is a rectangle of the art canvas, one physical piece of the wall. An output is a rectangle of the desktop, the physical pixels a fullscreen browser covers (two 4K ports side by side are a desktop of 7680 × 2160). A feed says which segment goes into which output, and where inside it. This is the room-corner example from packages/align/layouts/, two walls and the floor in front of them on one 4K output that a splitter cuts in four: jsonCopy key art{ w, h } in whole pixels; meters only when somebody measured (a number nobody measured does not go on the wall) segments[]{ id, x, y, w, h }; optional meters, color ('#hex' or a dark and a light one), cells.size, blend { l, r, t, b, curve, gamma } (a blend band, art px), masks (a door, an opening, in the segment's own px), label, plan (the number on a floor plan) outputs[]{ id, x, y, w, h } on the desktop, never overlapping; cuts { cols, rows } when a splitter cuts it feeds[]{ segment, output, x, y }; w, h when the output scales (an LED processor); rotate 0, 90, 180, 270 clockwise; one segment into two outputs is a stack (two projectors on one picture), each feed with its own name and color; visible when the room sees only part of it vendor[]the vendor's own alignment images, { file, output } or { file, rect }, any number paramsthe venue questions the layout was made from, each with a default and a note; status: "assumed" needs an ask: whom to ask, and what identthe identification screen's surfaces, their names, what is on each side, the order the band of light runs validateLayout() refuses a layout whose pixels are not whole numbers, whose segment leaves the canvas, whose outputs overlap, whose feed names nothing or lands outside its output, with every problem at once and where it is. It warns (accepts, but look) about a segment fed nowhere, two segments that overlap without a blend band, and metres whose pixels per metre across and down differ by more than 2 %, which on an LED wall is nearly always one number copied wrong. Before anything goes on the wall: bashCopy It prints the same, then where every tile lands, the stacks and blend bands, the masks, and the params still assumed with the question to ask. A file written as "contract": "art-align/v1", for the module this package grew from, loads as it is.

computeMapping(layout) turns the layout into one table of tiles, one per feed: src on the art canvas, dst on the desktop. Three things read only that table: The test patterns. drawPattern(ctx, mapping, pattern) draws tiles (a two-tone checkerboard per segment with cell names A1, B8 …, its name, size and metres, diagonals, a centre cross and circle), grid (a line every 100 art px, a heavy one every 500 with the absolute art coordinate), edges, crosshair (an ellipse means the proportions are wrong) and bars (smpte, steps, and a ramp across the whole canvas that shows a step between two segments of different brightness). Each tile is clipped to its place on the desktop and drawn in art pixels: the work's own path. The vendor's chart. drawChart(ctx, mapping, outputId) draws one 1:1 image per output for the hardware or splitter vendor: a grid with coordinates, the splitter's cuts and the range of each, every block's size and its first and last pixel, its masks, which side is the art's top, and "pixel to pixel, no scaling" in the header (or a warning when a block scales). vendorPlacements() lays the vendor's own images over the outputs where the layout says they are. The output. blitPlan() and createBlitter(THREE, renderer) copy the work's render target onto the desktop tile by tile, 1:1 or scaled; createWarpRenderer(THREE) does it through a calibration and can turn a feed. Why that is a guarantee and not a hope: a pattern is not a picture of what the wall should look like, it is drawn through the very tiles the work goes out through, and through the same warp (the align mode paints its patterns on the art canvas, drawSource(), and hands them to the same renderer as the work). If the cells pattern sits right on the wall, the work does. If the vendor's own image and the cells pattern disagree, the layout is wrong, not the wall: fix the file, and the patterns, the chart and the work move together.

A calibration (open-audiovisual/align-calibration@1) holds, for each tile, a zone: its four corners on the desktop (the segment's top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, in px), a mesh of 2 to 9 points a side that shifts the picture on top of that perspective (a curved or uneven surface), a feather on each edge (a share of the zone, for the overlap of two projectors), a gamma, a gain and black masks. An uncalibrated zone is exactly the layout's mapping. Each variant of a work's layout keeps its own zones in the same file, and a file written as art-align-cal/v1 loads as it is. normalizeCalibration(file, mapping) makes any file whole for a mapping: what cannot be read takes the default. jsCopy

Before you go. Write the layout, run node tools/check-align-layout.mjs on it, answer the assumed params you can, and send each vendor the chart of their output (drawChart at the output's full size, saved as a PNG: a scaled copy is not a chart). Ask the LED processor and the splitter to scale nothing. Arrive. Set the machine's displays to the layout's desktop, the same size and order, and open the work fullscreen across them. Show the identification screen (ident): every surface in its own colour with its name, which projector and which part of which output feeds it, what is on each side, and a band of light that runs along the walls in order. A wrong order or a wrong side shows here, before anything else. Pixels. Show tiles. Each segment's cells must be where the vendor's chart says, the cell names readable, a stack's two colours mixing evenly. A cell name in the wrong place is a layout or a processor setting, not a calibration. Corners. Enter the align mode and show grid or crosshair. For each zone (Tab, or a click), drag its four corners onto the surface's corners, or pick one with [ ] and move it with the arrows: 1 px, Shift 10, Alt 0.25. A corner that would fold the quad does not move. Mesh. A surface that is not flat: G, then drag the mesh points (+ − for more or fewer). Blend. Where two projectors overlap, show grey 50 % and feather (E) the overlapping side of each until the band is gone; gamma 2.2 is the usual start. Even out the brightness of a zone with , and .. Masks. K, then N adds one, the arrows place it and Shift resizes it. A door the layout lists is already masked. Check with the work. P back to the work, then the bars for black level (see 4 % and not 2 %), white for evenness, black for light leaking where nothing should be. Keep it. Every change is saved a second later (in the browser, with the last 20 saves as backups; in an app, files through a bridge). X exports the file to keep with the show, I imports one, L lists the backups. key (align mode) C, G, E, Kedit corners, mesh, feather, masks Tab, 1–9, clickpick a zone [ ]next handle (corners, mesh points, feather sides, masks) arrowsmove 1 px; Shift ×10, Alt ×0.25; masks: Shift resizes drag, Shift+draga handle; the whole zone + − · Q · N · , .mesh density · turn the zone 90° · add a mask · brightness P, Shift+P · Vthe next picture · the next layout variant O · J · Backspacehide the frames · move the panel · the handle home (Shift: the whole zone) ⌘S · ⌘Z · L · X · I · Asave · undo · backups · export · import · leave The panel speaks English, or Chinese with lang: 'zh'. The words drawn…

Gray code is how a camera can find which projector pixel lands where. Each axis of a projector needs one black-and-white stripe frame per bit of its coordinates, ceil(log2 size), each followed by its inverse (so every camera pixel gets its own threshold, whatever the light), after one white and one black frame: a 1920 × 1200 projector is 11 + 11 bits, 46 frames. Gray code, because a camera pixel on a stripe's edge that reads one bit wrong is then one projector pixel off, not half the picture. Channel separation: each projector draws only in its own colour channel, R, G or B, so three projectors run at once and one photo of each frame measures all three. A fourth projector takes a second pass (channelPlan). graySequence() lists the frames, drawGrayFrame() draws one over the desktop. They are drawn in output pixels, never through the calibration: what is measured is the projector itself. Example 31's Gray code button steps through them, [ and ], with each frame's name, on a scaled preview of the desktop: to shoot, draw them with drawGrayFrame(ctx, mapping, frame, { view: { k: 1, x: 0, y: 0 } }) on a canvas the desktop's size, fullscreen across the outputs, so every stripe is whole projector pixels. To shoot them: the camera on a tripod where it sees every surface, exposure, focus and white balance fixed by hand, the room dark, every projector on; one photo per frame, in the sequence's order, named after the frame (frameLabel()). Do not move the camera between frames.

The camera half. In order, what an automatic alignment would still need: stagewhathere 0the camera's intrinsics and distortion, the crosstalk between colour channelsnot built 1the frames (channel-separated Gray code); then capture, a threshold per camera pixel, the camera ↔ projector correspondencethe frames and the bits → coordinate arithmetic (decodeGrayBits) are built; the rest is not 2from the correspondence into the art canvas: what "right" means, right for a viewer standing here, or evenly spread on the surface (an artistic choice)not built 3blending: weights, a measured brightness field, black levelthe layout's blend bands (blendWeight) and the hand-set feather are built; a measured field and black level are not 4convergence: the residual in camera pixels as the stop conditionnot built 5save and reload: a measured result written into the same calibration filethe manual calibration file is built; a measured one is not Until then, the venue day above is the alignment.

Three packages export a validateLayout (surface's checks a phone control surface, tile's a layout.json, align's this layout) and two a normalizeLayout (surface, align). A page that uses two imports one under another name: import { validateLayout as validateAlignLayout } from '@openav/align'.

@openav/align is the alignment module art-align, made public. A work that copies art-align into its own folder can switch its import to @openav/align: the documented names keep their names and arguments, its layout and calibration files load as they are, and they are written back with the new format names. The words on the wall and the messages are English, Chinese with lang: 'zh'. createCalStore() keeps its files under the prefix oav-align; while nothing is saved there it reads art-align's art-align/* keys, so a calibration art-align saved is still found. Not here: the adapters to two earlier venue implementations (toLegacyMap, layoutFromQuery and their kin), the venue test page and its deploy tools.

Example 31 in headless Chromium 151 (Playwright 1.62), one machine, node serve.js, no permissions granted, three.js 0.170.0 from jsDelivr (packages/align/test/align-smoke.cjs): every example layout loads with no console error, its identification screen and its charts drawn, one warp mesh per tile; the picture list changes the warped canvas; a corner dragged with the mouse in the align mode moves the zone's corner by the distance dragged and changes the rendered picture; after a reload the corner is where it was left; the panel reads in Chinese when the guide is set to 中文; the Gray-code frames step in output pixels (frame 5 of 46, X bit 2 of 11). Not checked: a real projector, a real LED processor or splitter, a desktop of several physical outputs, the WebGL warp on a venue machine's graphics card, the Electron bridge of createCalStore, and any camera.

open-audiovisual models MIDI controllers as data: one JSON file per device, with the faceplate layout, every control's exact MIDI message, LED feedback, how to recognise its port, and the document each number came from. The same file drives an on-screen controller you can play, follows the real device when you plug it in, and can be dropped into any web page. Every device is on the controllers page.

htmlCopy That is the whole integration. The element works without Web MIDI (Safari, iPad): it plays and fires events; only hardware and MIDI out report that they are unavailable. It never asks for MIDI permission unless you turn on hardware, midi-out or learn. Safari has none because WebKit has not implemented it (bug 107250, still open). AttributeWhat it does profilewhich device: an id, a short name, or a URL to your own profile JSON layoutauto, face (as it looks) or stack (re-gridded for a phone held upright) hardwareon, or ask for a button: the real device moves the on-screen one midi-outa port name (IAC, loopMIDI), /regex/, or ask: what you play is sent there channel1–16, when your unit is set to another channel picker, readout, learn, followdevice picker, last-message line, learn button, show whatever known device you plug in

macOS: Audio MIDI Setup → Window → Show MIDI Studio → IAC Driver → “Device is online”. Windows 11: the built-in Windows MIDI Services (released 2026-02-17, rolled out in stages to 24H2 and 25H2) share MIDI ports between apps and include a loopback, and Microsoft's announcement says web pages using Web MIDI can use it (Windows blog). We have not tested it with open-audiovisual. Older Windows: install loopMIDI and add a port; that still works. <oav-controller profile="akai-lpd8" midi-out="IAC"> (on Windows, give the name of the port you made or the one Windows shows). In Ableton Live, turn on Track and Remote for that input; in TouchDesigner, a MIDI In CHOP on it; in Resolume, Preferences → MIDI. Hands on the screen are sent; your real hardware is not forwarded (the DAW already hears it). The engine never listens to IAC inputs, and the element mutes an input named like its output, so nothing loops.

So the project can see where its controllers and shows end up, the packages send one anonymous hit per page load to Google Analytics 4 (the openaudiovisual.com property, G-1YG2JHK2WT): eventwhenparams oav_embed_loadan <oav-controller>, createController() or the iframe startsoav_kind (element · headless · iframe), oav_profile, oav_host, oav_version oav_hardware_connecta real controller is plugged in and matchedoav_kind, oav_profile, oav_host, oav_version oav_show_startcreateShow() startsoav_kind (show), oav_host, oav_version oav_host is the origin of the page it runs on (for the iframe, the page that holds it), never the path, query or title. Nothing anyone plays is sent, no cookies are set, and the client id is random for every page load, so visitors can't be followed. No gtag.js is loaded: a page with its own Google Analytics keeps its dataLayer untouched. Nothing is sent from localhost, LAN addresses, file:// or openaudiovisual.com itself, or when the browser sends Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control. Turn it off: <oav-controller telemetry="off"> · createController(p, { telemetry: false }) · createShow({ telemetry: false }) · the iframe's ?telemetry=0 · or globalThis.OPENAV_TELEMETRY = false before anything loads. Source: packages/midi/telemetry.js. The one line for p5.js (oav-p5) sends nothing unless a sketch sets telemetry: 'on'. The signature is not a hit. createShow() also puts <meta name="generator" content="open-audiovisual 0.9.0"> in the page's head, the tag WordPress and Hugo leave. It makes no request: a person who views the source, a search of the public web or a web census can read which pages run on open-audiovisual, and that is all. createShow({ signature: false }) leaves it out. Source: packages/core/src/signature.js. Works that want to be listed by name add themselves to Made with.

openaudiovisual.com runs Google Analytics 4 on its own pages (the same property). Besides the page views Google Analytics counts by itself, assets/track.js counts nine things people do there, each as its own event: eventwhenparams oav_copya Copy button, or ⌘C / Ctrl+C inside a code blockkind (loader · code · import_map · other), page_type oav_outbounda link to another sitekind (github · vendor · work · course · openprocessing · other), host, page_type oav_controller_playthe first move on a page's on-screen controller, once per page viewcontroller, page_type oav_export_downloada QLC+, Mixxx or JSON file from a controller, fixture or device pageformat (qlc · mixxx · json), controller (the controller's, fixture's or device's id), page_type oav_example_startthe first click or key inside an example, once per page viewexample oav_next_stepa link in a page's next-step blockfrom (the page type), to (p5 · example · docs · reference · …) oav_searchthe first letter typed in a search box, once per page viewpage_type oav_lang_switchEN or 中文page_type, to (en · zh) oav_send_to_desktopthe button of the bar a phone shows, "Send this page to your computer"method (share · copy), page_type page_type says what kind of page it is: home, controller, controllers_index, verify, example, examples_index, docs, docs_chapter (/docs/<chapter>/), reference, reference_name (/docs/reference/<name>/), cheatsheet, p5, made_with, changelog, webtoe, check, not_found, devices_index (/devices/), fixture (/fixtures/<id>/) or device (/devices/<id>/). Each param is a short word or an id, never what was copied or typed into a search box, and never a link's path or query: host is the other site's name only. As with every page view, Google Analytics itself also records the page's address and sets its own cookie. The script runs only where the site's analytics runs, on openaudiovisual.com: not on localhost and not in a copy of the repository. Source: assets/track.js. None of this is in the framework. p5/oav-p5.js, packages/ and embed/ do not load the script and send nothing new, so a page someone else builds with open-audiovisual sends only what the first table lists. tests/track.test.js checks both.

Some things only SysEx can do: put a Launchpad in Programmer mode, pick a Launch Control XL template, light a pad in any RGB colour. Profiles that have these list them in sysex, each message with its source, and the device's page shows them. The browser shows a permission prompt for SysEx, so nothing in this project asks by itself: <oav-controller sysex> adds a button, and controller.enableSysex() is the call behind it (run it from a click). Once it is on, the device is set up every time it connects, and setLedColor(id, { r, g, b }) and sendSysex(id) work. Package README.

Every device page has the same data as a QLC+ input profile (.qxi) and a Mixxx mapping (.midi.xml and a small .js), and node tools/export-controller.mjs <id> writes them from any profile. The Mixxx mapping is a starting point: remap it with Mixxx's Learning Wizard. The library also lists controllers imported from QLC+'s input profiles, with generated layouts and every control marked unverified.

Copy the closest file in packages/midi/profiles/, or a generic layout. Write each control's type and message from the manual's MIDI implementation chart. Cite every source; mark anything unconfirmed "verified": false with a note. "verified": true is for a number checked on a real unit, and needs an entry in verifications that says who, when, on which firmware, OS and browser (validateProfile refuses it otherwise). validateProfile(profile) lists every problem; npm test checks every shipped profile. Try it with <oav-controller profile="./my-device.json">, then register it in profiles/index.js and open a pull request. No manual: choose a generic layout, press Learn, move your controls in order, and keep controller.exportMapping() as the start of a profile. The format has room for what a device does beyond notes and CCs: sysex (mode switches, templates, LED colours, each message citing its source), palette (the LED colour table) and verifications (who checked what on real hardware). The field list is in the package README, and profile.schema.json is the same format as JSON Schema.

The things a show plugs in are many kinds of thing: a MIDI controller, a par can, an LED strip, a camera, an audio interface, a hand sensor, a sensor wired to a board. OAV already speaks to most of them, each through its own package and its own file format. @openav/devices puts them in one collection with one outer record, so a page, a tool or an agent can list them, search them, and ask for any one of them by id, and get it back ready for the package that drives it. jsCopy

A profile, a fixture and a part stay in their own files, the only place their facts are written, and the collection's record of each one is read off that file: when the package is built (node tools/build-devices.mjs writes packages/devices/catalog.js, the list devices() answers from) and again when device() loads it. A test fails when a profile, a fixture or a part exists that the list does not have, and when the list says something its file no longer does. Listing is cheap. devices() reads one generated file, so a page can show and search the whole collection without fetching every profile; device() imports the one file the device lives in. The first hand-written records are gear the project has on the desk, so each can be checked on the unit: the Yamaha AG06, the Logitech MX Brio, the Audinate Dante Virtual Soundcard, the Ultraleap Leap Motion Controller 2, WLED, the ENTTEC DMX USB Pro and the Brother QL-810W. The collection is on the site: /devices/ lists every device by kind, with a filter and a search. A controller's page stays at /controllers/<id>/; each DMX fixture has one at /fixtures/<id>/ (every mode's channel table, a virtual fixture, the patch code, the file), and a record or a part at /devices/<id>/ (the facts with their sources, setup, problems, the code, the file; a camera or an audio input can be looked for from the page, behind a button). A device gets a page of its own when it offers at least two of: something to try on screen, code that reaches it, a file to take. The Brother QL-810W has only its record, so it stays a row of the list until OAV has code for it.

Every device has the same outer record, open-audiovisual/device@1, described by device.schema.json for software that does not run this package. field id, kind, manufacturer, namewho it is. manufacturer is null when the file it is read from names no maker (the parts library, the generic layouts) aliaseswhat people type when they search for it: a short name, the Chinese name, a model number connections, protocolshow it plugs in (usb, din-midi, ethernet, wifi, dmx-xlr5, …) and what it speaks (midi, dmx512, art-net, …). Each snippet runs as a module in a page whose import map is the examples' one plus "@openav/devices": "../../packages/devices/index.js". Only the camera's button asks for a permission, and only when it is clicked.

routes() is @openav/midi's controllerRoutes: mapper routes from the controller's named signals to your params. addTo() puts the profile into a MidiControllers and returns its live controller. The unit is recognised by its port name when the manager gets its hardware engine (controllers.attach(midi)) and at each device change, so call addTo() first: a unit already plugged in is otherwise matched the next time a device comes or goes. jsCopy
patch() places the fixture in a @openav/dmx Patch. The id defaults to <device>-<universe>-<address>, the universe to 1, the mode to the profile's first. jsCopy
jsCopy

The device is found among the browser's media devices by its label. constraints() is pure. find() calls enumerateDevices() and returns the device or null. open() is the only call that asks for a permission, so call it from a click. jsCopy Browsers hide the labels until the page has had the permission once, so before that find() returns null; open() then asks, looks again, and if the browser opened another camera first, closes it and opens this one. With the labels visible and no match, it throws with the names it found and asks for nothing. An audio interface opens with echo cancellation, noise suppression and auto gain off, as @openav/audio asks a microphone; feed it to an analyzer with analyzer.input().context.createMediaStreamSource(stream).connect(analyzer.input()). @openav/pose opens the default camera itself, so a found camera does not reach the pose trackers yet.
A sensor, an LED controller, a DMX interface or a printer comes back as its record. Its use names the package and the call that reach it: jsCopy

A device that has a deeper format goes there: a MIDI controller is a profile (MIDI controllers), a light is a fixture (DMX lighting), a part goes into packages/hw/parts.js. The collection picks it up. Anything else is a record: packages/devices/records/<id>.json, the file name being the id. Copy one of the same kind. Run node tools/build-devices.mjs: it validates every record and rewrites catalog.js. Then node --test tests/devices.test.js. Leave verified false and verifications empty. Only a person with the unit can make it true.

Every fact cites the page it was read from. A number, a port, a protocol name, a sample rate, a resolution comes from the manufacturer's own page or manual, with its URL in sources and the day it was read. What could not be read on such a page is left out, or written in tbd, never guessed. A short honest record beats a full guessed one. Facts and links only. No manual prose, no product photos: a manufacturer's page is under copyright, its facts are not. Setup steps and known problems come from the manufacturer's documents or from this handbook (troubleshooting, the package notes), each citing which. Label patterns (how a camera or an audio input is found by name) are written from the model name until someone reads the label a browser shows on a unit; each record says so in tbd. Licences. A record is MIT, like the project. A record read off a profile, a fixture or a part takes that file's licence: the controllers imported from QLC+ are Apache-2.0 (see NOTICE). Data from Mixxx (GPL) and midi.guide (CC-BY-SA) does not come in.

OP Configurator 3000 (OPC, built into OpenProcessing) names a variable and its range. With this line on the page the controller is wired to those variables in order, with no mapping step: jsCopy Knobs drive the sliders in the order they are declared, the faders continue after the knobs, and pads drive toggles and buttons. OPC's panel moves with the knob, and parameterChanged() fires as usual. OpenProcessing's OPC panel can also learn hardware by itself (its MIDI switch); once that mapping is seen working, hardware is left to it and this line keeps wiring the on-screen controller and the phone, which OpenProcessing cannot see. Avoid OPC names that are also p5 functions (hue, fill): p5 1.x clashes with them. One knob, one job. If the sketch also reads knob1 itself, knob 1 is the sketch's: the first OPC slider no longer follows it (drag it on OPC's panel), the other knobs stay wired, and a hint says so once. The first line of the 🎹 panel is the wiring, for example knob1 → knob1 (sketch; radius by its slider) · knob2 → speed (OPC).

The same line reads the microphone, and the sketch reads it the same way: as variables. jsCopy readvalue micLevel0..1, how loud it sounds: the room's own noise is 0, talking is about 0.4–0.6, shouting is near 1 bass, mid, treble0..1, the energy in 20–250 Hz, 250–2000 Hz and 2000–8000 Hz beattrue for one frame per beat, like mouseIsPressed while a button is down micIsOnwhether the microphone is running startMic(), stopMic()turn it on or off from code (they return a promise) micSensitivity(2)twice as sensitive; micSensitivity() returns the current value write this functionwhen it is called beatDetected(level)a beat: a jump in loudness over what the room has been doing (level 0..1) kickDetected(level), snareDetected(level), hatDetected(level)a hit in the low, middle or high band (20–120 Hz, 150–800 Hz, 6–14 kHz) It is off until the sketch asks. Nothing is requested when the page loads. The first time the sketch reads micLevel, bass, mid, treble or beat, or calls startMic(), the browser asks for the microphone; until the answer arrives every value is 0. A sketch that defines beatDetected() and reads nothing starts it on the first click or key. In the 🎹 panel the 🎤 button turns it on and off by hand and shows the level, and it says so when the browser blocked the microphone (click it again after allowing it from the address bar). Click first, if the browser wants one. Browsers keep audio quiet until the page has been clicked. This file asks as soon as draw() reads a value and starts the microphone again on the first click or key if the browser held it back, so no userStartAudio() is needed. Next to p5.sound. The analysis is @openav/audio (an AnalyserNode), loaded from next to this file the first time it is needed, with its own AudioContext. p5.sound (p5.AudioIn, p5.FFT) can run on the same page; the two microphones do not share anything, and none of these names is a p5 or p5.sound name. It works in p5 1.x and 2.x global mode. How loud is loud. micLevel is a loudness in decibels, measured from the room: its bottom follows the room's own noise (it settles in a second or two, and rises at most 1.5 dB a second, so a voice never becomes the new silence), and −10 dBFS, shouting into a laptop, is 1. So 50 + micLevel * 300 visibly grows when someone talks. A quiet or far microphone: micSensitivity(3) (+9.5 dB on micLevel, ×3 on the bands, still capped at 1). The raw numbers are OAVp5.mic.rms (0..1), OAVp5.mic.db and OAVp5.mic.floor (the room, in dBFS). OAVp5.mic.on('beat', fn) is the same as defining beatDetected, and returns a function that stops it.
